items.descriptionOriginal: When we vote in a national or state election, we often have a document to refer to: the political party's manifesto. It tells us what the party promises to do if elected, from creating jobs and improving healthcare to building infrastructure. And once the government is in power, those promises give voters something to question it about. "But what happens when we vote for our village's Gram Pradhan? What are the promises we can expect them to make? And, more importantly, what can we hold them accountable for once they are elected?" This is the question that IAS officer Dr Heera Lal wants to bring into village elections through a 25-point Village Manifesto. His idea is straightforward: village elections, too, should be fought on issues and written promises, giving people a clearer say in what development should look like in their communities. "Elections are contested in Parliament on manifestos. In MLA seats, on manifestos. But in the village, we do not have any manifesto," he explains. A village's priorities could begin with a blocked drain, an unresolved land dispute or something as basic as sanitation. For him, a manifesto is essentially a written promise . If a candidate commits to addressing specific problems before being elected, villagers have something tangible to refer to afterwards. Without such a commitment, he argues, it becomes difficult for voters to question their elected representative about what they have delivered. Beyond roads, schools and drinking Water The 25-point framework tries to broaden what villages consider development. Conversations around rural progress often centre on a handful of visible needs, such as roads, schools, drinking water and electricity. But several other factors shape a village's quality of life, too. Saurabh Lall, CEO of Model Gaon, which developed the framework , says the idea emerged from recognising that a better life could not be measured through just three or four parameters. "Our first initiative was to make them understand that a better life entails a lot many other things than just having these three, four things being worked upon," he says. The manifesto therefore looks at a wider range of issues, including health, education, sanitation, income generation, employment, access to technology, sustainability, women's empowerment, local talent, dispute resolution and proper documentation of village records. Solar power, better sanitation and access to technology feature among the 25 priorities proposed for village-level development. Some of these priorities may not immediately come to mind when people think about rural development. But they can have a direct bearing on everyday life. A village where small disputes repeatedly escalate into expensive legal cases, for instance, faces a different challenge from one where the most pressing concern is access to irrigation or employment. The framework was deliberately simplified into a one-page document so that villagers could understand and engage with it. It was also designed to be personalised. "All those 25 things could mean different things for different people. And their priorities in life would also differ based on the phase of life that they were in, the context that they were living in," says Saurabh. The idea, then, is not to impose the same development agenda on every village. It is to give communities a framework through which they can identify what matters most to them. What should your village's manifesto actually promise? A list of 25 priorities is only a starting point . The more important exercise is deciding which of those priorities need attention first in a particular village. To do this, the process involves conversations at the ward level, where residents can raise problems they experience in their everyday lives. These meetings typically bring together around 25 to 35 people from a particular part of the village. The concerns can be remarkably specific. Saurabh recalls residents raising issues such as a drain being constructed inconveniently outside someone's home or a neighbour encroaching on a portion of their land. One recurring concern was the number of small local disputes that were escalating into court cases. Residents often had to travel to cities, spend money, and wait for lengthy legal processes to resolve issues that could potentially be addressed locally. Ward-level meetings bring 25 to 35 residents together to discuss everyday problems and decide which issues deserve attention first. "If people stop wasting time in resolving their petty disputes, they would end up either studying or working in their farms or looking for jobs," he says. In such cases, dispute resolution could become one of the village's most important priorities, even if it might not feature prominently in another village's manifesto. The meetings also allow the Gram Pradhan to hear these concerns directly. Rather than treating the manifesto as a document prepared by an outside organisation, the aim is to make it a reflection of what residents themselves want addressed. Saurabh believes this participation is essential to meaningful development. "Unless and until the beneficiary is involved in the designing of the programme itself, it never really gets very comprehensive." From written promises to accountability For a manifesto to mean something beyond election season, its promises must translate into action. That requires villagers to know what their priorities are, and their elected representatives to understand how to work towards them. Saurabh says the process also involves helping Gram Pradhans understand their rights, responsibilities, and the administrative procedures involved in local governance. The aim is to help them identify solutions by bringing together existing government schemes, local resources and relevant expertise. "We said that installing another system is not the solution. Galvanising the existing system is probably going to be more effective," he says. What should a Gram Pradhan promise voters? The manifesto encourages residents to identify their most pressing local needs. This is important because a village's problems do not always require an entirely new project or a fresh allocation of funds. Sometimes, the challenge is knowing which existing resources can be brought together to address a particular need. The larger ambition is to take this framework into upcoming Gram Pradhan elections. Dr Heera Lal describes the campaign with a slogan: "Chunaav mudra se nahi, muddon pe hoga" — elections should be fought on issues, not money. The proposal is to make the village manifesto a part of the election conversation, so candidates can put their priorities in writing and voters can assess them against the needs of their communities. Ultimately, the 25-point framework raises a question that goes beyond any one organisation or development initiative: shouldn't people have a clearer say in what their elected village representatives promise to deliver? A manifesto cannot guarantee that every problem will be solved. But it can give a village something to begin with: a shared list of priorities, written commitments and a way to ask its elected representative what has been done.

items.title: 8 από τις πιο εντυπωσιακές φωτογραφίες από το τεύχος του National Geographic, Pictures of the Year 2026
items.titleOriginal: 8 of the most stunning photos from National Geographic’s Pictures of the Year 2026 issue
items.description: Οι φωτογράφοι του National Geographic ταξιδεύουν σε όλο τον κόσμο για να μας δείξουν τα θαύματα του φυσικού κόσμου από προοπτικές που είναι σχεδόν αδύνατο να αποτυπωθούν οπουδήποτε αλλού. Οι φωτογράφοι του κατέγραψαν πάνω από ένα εκατομμύριο φωτογραφίες το 2026 και πρόσφατα αποκάλυψε το Pictures of the Year 2026, μια συλλογή από 25 εξαιρετικές φωτογραφίες που αποκαλύπτουν τη μαμά…
items.descriptionOriginal: National Geographic’ s photographers travel across the globe to show us the wonders of the natural world from perspectives that are nearly impossible to capture anywhere else. Its photographers captured over a million images in 2026, and it recently unveiled Pictures of the Year 2026, a collection of 25 extraordinary photographs that reveal the moments, discoveries, and untold stories that defined the past year. The images will transport viewers from deep within the chilly waters of Greenland to see an incredible shark, to the Chankillo Solar Observatory in Casma, Peru, for a rare view of the sun. They’ll also get to visit the Italian Alps to meet a charming horse that loves hats. “The power of photography is that it makes visible and understandable things many of us would never otherwise see, and that it can help us view something familiar in an entirely new way,” Nathan Lump, editor-in-chief of National Geographic , said in a statement. “This year’s PICTURES OF THE YEAR collection is a testament to the boundless curiosity and relentless persistence of our photographers in their quest to help us better understand our world. Together, these images remind us how much there is still to discover about our planet, and that the deeply human work of documenting what’s real is more valuable than ever in a time when fakes are everywhere.” Here are eight of our favorite photos from National Geographic’s Pictures of the Year 2026. 1 . Pygmy Whale Lunge by Ralph Pace In New Zealand’s warming waters, a pygmy whale lunges, mouth agape, to feed on abundant krill. Although the giant species is ordinarily migratory, some 700 of them have settled here. Photographer Ralph Pace dived with researchers studying how climate change affects the krill and, in turn, the whales’ feeding and breeding. (Photo by Ralph Pace) “In New Zealand’s warming waters, a pygmy whale lunges, mouth agape, to feed on abundant krill. Although the giant species is ordinarily migratory, some 700 of them have settled here. Photographer Ralph Pace dived with researchers studying how climate change affects the krill and, in turn, the whales’ feeding and breeding.” 2. The Path of the Sun in Peru by Diego López Calvín Apparent path of the sun as seen from the western observation point at the Chankillo Solar Observatory in Casma (Ankash), Peru. The six-month-long continuous exposure (solarigraphy) taken between June 21 and December 21, 2025, accurately shows the sun’s path, with the winter and summer solstices located at the ends of the structure outlined by the silhouette of the towers. (Photo by Diego López Calvín) “Apparent path of the sun as seen from the western observation point at the Chankillo Solar Observatory in Casma (Ankash), Peru. The six-month-long continuous exposure (solarigraphy) taken between June 21 and December 21, 2025, accurately shows the sun’s path, with the winter and summer solstices located at the ends of the structure outlined by the silhouette of the towers.” 3. A Tribute to Those We Lost on 9/11 Photo by Christopher Payne Every September for the past 25 years, a crew has lit up New York’s night sky to commemorate those who died during the attack on the World Trade Center’s twin towers. Christopher Payne combined four images to capture these technicians setting up the 9/11 “Tribute in Light,” which forms two beams visible 60 miles away—a symbol of the city’s resilience. (Photo by Christopher Payne) “Every September for the past 25 years, a crew has lit up New York’s night sky to commemorate those who died during the attack on the World Trade Center’s twin towers. Christopher Payne combined four images to capture these technicians setting up the 9/11 ‘Tribute in Light,’ which forms two beams visible 60 miles away—a symbol of the city’s resilience.” 4. A Hat for a Horse by Jasper Doest Lorena Masei playfully offers her hat to a horse at the Masei family farm in the Italian Alps. Photographer Jasper Doest was in the mountains to document how communities there coexist with wild animals but found himself struck by the family’s relationship to livestock they’re raising in a landscape shared by bears and wolves. (Photo by Jasper Doest) “Lorena Masei playfully offers her hat to a horse at the Masei family farm in the Italian Alps. Photographer Jasper Doest was in the mountains to document how communities there coexist with wild animals but found himself struck by the family’s relationship to livestock they’re raising in a landscape shared by bears and wolves.” 5. Future of Farming by Brent Stirton Frankie and Joey Druffel play among the compost mounds on their family’s farm. Their dad, Allen, a fifth-generation farmer, uses modernized forms of herbicide-and pesticide free methods—drawing from the practices of his great-great-grandfather—and has implemented soil restoration techniques to quell weeds and add nutrients without chemicals. (Photo by Brent Stirton) “Frankie and Joey Druffel play among the compost mounds on their family’s farm. Their dad, Allen, a fifth-generation farmer, uses modernized forms of herbicide- and pesticide-free methods—drawing from the practices of his great-great-grandfather—and has implemented soil restoration techniques to quell weeds and add nutrients without chemicals.” 6. A Greenland Shark by Kiliii Yüyan A Greenland shark, the oldest vertebrate on earth, swims underneath the meter-thick sea ice near the village of Kulusuk in East Greenland, as diver Philipp Oppermann watches. This shark came up from the depths into the shallows at night to follow the scent of a Greenlander's bait, frozen ringed seal. This photograph was made March 17, 2026, in early spring, when the sea ice remains strong and the visibility of the water is spectacular, over 50 meters. (Photo by Kiliii Yüyan) “A Greenland shark, the oldest vertebrate on earth, swims underneath the meter-thick sea ice near the village of Kulusuk in East Greenland, as diver Philipp Oppermann watches. This shark came up from the depths into the shallows at night to follow the scent of a Greenlander’s bait, frozen ringed seal. This photograph was made March 17, 2026, in early spring, when the sea ice remains strong and he visibility of the water is spectacular, over 50 meters.” 7. Monkey Business by Prakash Matada A curious troop of Gee’s golden langurs—named for a naturalist who documented them in the 1950s—peer into a fisheye lens that Prakash Matada affixed to a tele scoping pole. The endangered canopy dwellers here have formed a rare bond with humans and proved anything but camera shy, gazing at their own reflections.(Photo by Prakash Matada) “A curious troop of Gee’s golden langurs—named for a naturalist who documented them in the 1950s—peer into a fisheye lens that Prakash Matada affixed to a telescoping pole. The endangered canopy dwellers here have formed a rare bond with humans and proved anything but camera-shy, gazing at their own reflections.” 8. A Hard Day’s Rest by Matthieu Paley Twenty-six years ago, photographer Matthieu Paley first visited Afghanistan’s Wakhan corridor, a narrow strip of land bordering Pakistan, Tajikistan, and China—and was trans fixed. Repeated visits have only deepened his connection to the region and the local Wakhi people. Here, Hazal-u Din reclines by firelight after a long day herding yaks. (Photo by Matthieu Paley) “Twenty-six years ago, photographer Matthieu Paley first visited Afghanistan’s Wakhan corridor, a narrow strip of land bordering Pakistan, Tajikistan, and China—and was trans fixed. Repeated visits have only deepened his connection to the region and the local Wakhi people. Here, Hazal-u Din reclines by firelight after a long day herding yaks.” For more on this story, visit NatGeo.com/Photos . The December 2026 cover of National Geographic . items.descriptionOriginal: On Dec. 15, 1997, a fire tore through Luz Cuevas’ home in Philadelphia. She got out with two of her sons. When she ran back for her 10-day-old daughter, Delimar, the crib was empty. Fire investigators blamed a space heater cord. They never found any remains and concluded the blaze had consumed the baby. Cuevas never quite believed it. Six years later, in January 2004, she went to a child’s birthday party at the home of a relative of Delimar’s father. A 6-year-old girl with deep dimples caught her eye. The girl’s name was Aaliyah, and she came with Carolyn Correa, who was related to the family by marriage and had visited Cuevas’ home the day of the fire. Cuevas followed the girl upstairs, told her she had gum in her hair, and pulled out five strands. She folded them into a napkin, sealed them in a plastic bag, and locked them in a safe. “Because of TV, I knew they needed hair for the DNA,” she told reporters at the time, according to CBS News . The DNA matched, meaning Aaliyah was Delimar. Investigators concluded that Correa had taken the baby and set the fire to cover it up. Correa pleaded no contest to kidnapping, interfering with custody, and conspiracy in 2005 and was paroled in 2013. Delimar was reunited with her mother in March 2004. She’s an adult now, and she’s been telling her side of the story, including in the 2023 documentary The Hand That Robbed the Cradle. On Tamron Hall that spring, she said she remembered the party: the woman in the hallway, Correa’s panic, the rush to leave. She also said that when the DNA test came, Correa took her into a bathroom and sprayed something into her mouth, which she later came to believe was an attempt to contaminate the sample with Correa’s own saliva. She’s also convinced Correa didn’t act alone. “I know that she didn’t take me out of that window by herself,” she has said. “There’s definitely somebody out there that assisted her. But, whoever it was, Carolyn is protecting that person with her life.” The post Her baby supposedly died in a house fire. Six years later, she spotted her at a birthday party. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: The ‘Frasier’ theme song sounds like a dinner order. Its composer was given a problem to solve.
items.description: Ως μακροχρόνιος θαυμαστής του Frasier, μπορώ να τραγουδήσω το θεματικό τραγούδι στον ύπνο μου. «Ω, μωρό μου, ακούω τα blues a-callin», πεταμένες σαλάτες και ομελέτα…» Πάντα πίστευα ότι το μέρος με τις σαλάτες -και- τα αυγά ήταν ανόητο και δεν σκέφτηκα ποτέ να σκάψω άλλο. Αλλά αποδεικνύεται ότι οι στίχοι του θέματος Frasier δεν είναι καθόλου ανόητοι. Σε συνέντευξή του στην Paramount…
items.descriptionOriginal: As a long-time fan of Frasier , I can sing the theme song in my sleep. “ Oh baby, I hear the blues a-callin’, tossed salads and scrambled eggs… ” I always assumed the salads -and- eggs part was nonsensical and never thought to dig any further. But it turns out the lyrics of the Frasier theme aren’t nonsensical at all. In an interview with Paramount Plus , the song’s composer, Bruce Miller, explained how the lyrics came about and why they are actually perfectly fitting for the show. What do tossed salads and scrambled eggs have to do with psychology? Frasier , which originally ran for 11 seasons before getting a two-season revival in 2023-2024, follows psychologist Frasier Crane (from the original Cheers sitcom) after he moves from Boston to Seattle. When Miller was tasked with writing the theme song, the show’s creators said they wanted something jazzy. But the instructions for the lyrics posed a challenge. “I remember David Angell saying, ‘Don’t mention Seattle, don’t mention Frasier, don’t mention psychiatrists, don’t mention anything having to do with the show. But make it germane to the show,'” Miller said. Miller called up Darryl Phinnessee to write the lyrics. He came up with “tossed salads and scrambled eggs” because they’re “mixed up,” just like the people who call into Frasier’s radio show for help. They weren’t just random foods thrown into the song for fun; they were an intentional metaphor for emotional and psychological turmoil. Pretty brilliant, actually. How Kelsey Grammer ended up singing the Frasier theme song himself Grammer wasn’t asked to sing the theme song. He simply decided to do it. “I actually said to the producers, ‘Oh, by the way, I’m gonna sing this song,’ ’cause I always wanted to sing a theme song. I thought, ‘Well, it’s my time. This is the only shot I’ll ever have.’ So I told them, ‘I’m doing the theme song.’ And they said, ‘Well, okay.'” “It’s nice when you have an actor that can sing,” added Miller. Grammer clearly had fun with it, and his performance definitely added to the series. He also said he loved what the song said about the character he was playing. “The thing I liked about the original spirit of the theme song, what we ended up having, was the fact that he’s always discovering life,” said Grammer. “That it’s always confusing. There’s always something that’s gonna surprise you, but he’s gonna figure it out. And that’s what I liked. You know, ‘I got you pegged.’ It’s gonna be okay. I mean, I got this.” This is why Frasier is my favorite show. Best moment. pic.twitter.com/v96drBuBKZ — Ali Hayati (@FollowHayati) December 15, 2022 The theme song exemplifies what made Frasier so good To keep a show going for 11 seasons is no small feat. You have to hit on all fronts to pull that off, and Frasier did. But the writing is really what made it stand out. It was smart and sophisticated, yet hilariously down-to-earth. The show’s writers deliberately refused to write down to their audience. In 2018, writer-producer Jon Sherman told Vanity Fair , “Someone on another show once told me about writing jokes, ‘You have to put a little kibble where the slow dogs can get it.’ That was never the consideration here.” David Lee, who co-created and directed Frasier , added, “We decided there could be jokes that not everyone got. We called them ’10 percenters.’ As long as we were delivering high quality for the other 90 percent, it was fine.” Their mantra: “No stupid jokes, no stupid characters. Deliver smart, heartfelt content framed within awkward situations. And never take the easy way out.” “Tossed Salads and Scrambled Eggs” isn’t an easy, obvious metaphor for psychology. It is, however, the kind of clever writing that kept people hooked for 11 years and has fans like me rewatching the show decades later. You can watch the classic Frasier series and the revival seasons on Paramount Plus. The post The ‘Frasier’ theme song sounds like a dinner order. Its composer was given a problem to solve. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Most of us are so caught up in the routines of everyday life that we forget even the most ordinary day has a story to tell. Most of that story is made up of things we barely notice: the coffee we make in the morning, the keys we grab on our way out the door, the phone we check between meetings. Countless objects we pick up and use during our normal routines can seem insignificant on their own. But taken together, they trace the shape of a day and reveal just how much is happening in the background of our everyday lives. That’s the idea behind photographer and ethnographer Paula Zuccotti ’s Every Thing We Touch project. It’s a fascinating collection of portraits made entirely from objects people handled over a 24-hour period. View this post on Instagram Zuccotti traveled around the world, asking people of all ages, professions, and backgrounds to keep track of everything they touched for a day. Her subjects included a toddler in Tokyo, a cowboy in Arizona, and a tile maker and designer in Marrakech. Just to name a few. She then gathered those objects together and neatly arranged them chronologically on a large canvas before photographing the entire collection from above. Zuccotti was careful about what counted. She left out large or permanent objects, such as sofas, cars, door handles, and light switches, because she wanted to focus on the movable things people actually interacted with throughout their day. The objects become a visual timeline The resulting photographs look almost like puzzles, inviting you to mentally reconstruct the day of the person who interacted with all the things we would normally take for granted. View this post on Instagram View this post on Instagram View this post on Instagram Some collections contain familiar items that show up in many people’s daily routines. Others offer clues about activities that are more specific to that person. The fun is in studying those details and imagining the story behind them. The project also raises an interesting question about what we can (and can’t) truly learn from someone’s possessions. What could our objects say about us? Zuccotti would later create the documentary Future Archeology , which imagines how people in the future might piece together our lives from the objects we leave behind. Archaeologists already do this, using leftover relics to piece together clues about how entire civilizations lived. But even with a whole day’s worth of evidence, there are limits to what a photograph can reveal. An object can tell us that someone touched it, but it can’t necessarily tell us why. We bring our own experiences and assumptions to what we see, which means two people might look at the same collection and imagine very different stories. And that’s one of the most intriguing aspects of Every Thing We Touch . The photographs let us get remarkably close to a stranger’s everyday life while leaving just enough mystery to remind us that we can never know the whole story from the outside. After all, if someone photographed everything you touched in a day, how much of your story would they actually capture? The post She photographed what people touched in a day. The objects tell surprisingly personal stories. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Μία από τις πιο γνωστές φωνές στο «Gimme Shelter» ανήκε σε έναν τραγουδιστή που φώναξε από το κρεβάτι
items.titleOriginal: One of the most familiar voices on ‘Gimme Shelter’ belonged to a singer called out of bed
items.description: Η επιτυχία των Rolling Stones του 1969 «Gimme Shelter» περιλαμβάνει μια από τις πιο αξέχαστες φωνητικές παραστάσεις της ροκ μουσικής και δεν είναι του Μικ Τζάγκερ. Ο Backup τραγουδιστής Merry Clayton κλήθηκε να σηκωθεί από το κρεβάτι στη μέση της νύχτας για να συμμετάσχει στο συγκρότημα σε ένα στούντιο ηχογράφησης του Λος Άντζελες. items.descriptionOriginal: The Rolling Stones’ 1969 hit “Gimme Shelter” features one of rock music’s most unforgettable vocal performances, and it isn’t Mick Jagger’s. Backup singer Merry Clayton was called out of bed in the middle of the night to join the band in a Los Angeles recording studio. Clayton was pregnant and knew little about the Rolling Stones beyond the fact that they were English. Her performance became one of the song’s defining moments . As she pushed her voice to its limits, Jagger shouted his approval in the background. His reaction can still be heard on the recording if you know where to listen. In a clip from the documentary 20 Feet from Stardom , Clayton listens to her isolated vocals and recalls that late-night recording session. Merry Clayton got a late-night call to sing with the Rolling Stones While finishing “Gimme Shelter,” the Rolling Stones wanted a woman’s voice for some of the song’s most unsettling lyrics. Producer Jack Nitzsche called Clayton’s home after she had already climbed into bed with her hair in curlers. “Merry, there’s a group of guys in town called Rolling…rolling somebodies, and they’re from England,” Clayton recalled in the documentary. “They picked me up with silk pajamas on, a mink coat, and a Chanel scarf on my head,” she added. The lyrics gave her pause. The song describes violence and destruction, including the repeated warning that rape and murder were “just a shot away.” In a 2013 interview with the A.V. Club , she described what was going through her mind as she sang, saying, “In my head is hoses and dogs being put on people, and I’m seeing the war in Vietnam and all this stuff is going on in my spirit while I’m singing this song.” “I’m just screaming to the world, and I guess that scream and that strain on my voice just cracked like a cry to the world,” she continued. Listen closely to “Gimme Shelter” and you’ll hear Mick Jagger’s reaction Clayton’s voice cracks as she reaches for a high note, and almost immediately, another voice shouts in the background. It’s Mick Jagger, reacting with an enthusiastic “Woo!” The moment can be easy to miss under the guitars and drums, but it’s much clearer when Clayton’s vocals are isolated from the rest of the recording. Without the instruments competing for attention, listeners can hear both the strain in her voice and Jagger’s excited response. The story behind the voice on “Gimme Shelter” For Clayton, the recording also carries a painful memory. She suffered a miscarriage the day after the session. In a 2021 interview with The Guardian , she attributed the loss to the physical strain of that night, though the connection has not been medically established. Clayton’s career extended well beyond her work with the Rolling Stones. She sang with artists including Ray Charles and Carole King and released her own recordings. Yet, like many backup singers, her voice was often more recognizable than her name. Her story received renewed attention through 20 Feet from Stardom , the 2013 documentary about backup singers who sang on some of popular music’s biggest hits. The film gave Clayton a chance to tell her own story, including how she came to record one of the Rolling Stones’ most famous songs. The post One of the most familiar voices on ‘Gimme Shelter’ belonged to a singer called out of bed appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Psychologists explain 6 traits of people who have kept friends for 20 years
items.description: Οι φιλίες απαιτούν ένα βασικό στοιχείο για να αναπτυχθούν: τον χρόνο που περνάτε μαζί. Μια μελέτη του 2019 που δημοσιεύτηκε στο Journal of Social and Personal Relationships παρατήρησε πόσες ώρες χρειάζονται για να αναπτυχθούν διαφορετικά επίπεδα φιλιών. Οι ερευνητές ανακάλυψαν ότι οι γνωστοί έγιναν περιστασιακοί φίλοι μετά από 50 ώρες μαζί. Χρειάστηκαν 90 ώρες για να επιτευχθεί η πραγματική ετικέτα o…
items.descriptionOriginal: Friendships require one key element to grow: time spent together. A 2019 study published in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships observed how many hours it takes for different levels of friendships to develop. Researchers found that acquaintances became casual friends after 50 hours together. It took 90 hours to achieve the true label of “friend,” and 200 hours to reach the title of a “close” friend. People who have maintained friendships for 20 years have invested time in those relationships, demonstrating a deep commitment to one another. “Commitment is a skill, and they practice it consistently, even when life gets busy,” Dr. Alexia Holovatyk , Ph.D., a licensed clinical psychologist in Los Angeles, tells Upworthy. View this post on Instagram Personality traits of people with 20-year friendships Maintaining long-term friendships requires consistent communication. “Most of these friendships aren’t kept alive by big gestures. They run on small, boring contact: the text about a song, the birthday call, the ‘saw this and thought of you,'” Alexis Sturnick , LCSW, PMH-C, founder and clinical director of Resilience Therapy in New York, tells Upworthy. “It looks like nothing, and it’s everything.” In addition to the “small, boring contact,” people who have kept friendships alive for 20 years tend to possess these six personality traits: Personality trait No. 1: They are flexible Phil Glickman , Licensed Clinical Psychologist and Owner of Wellness Road Psychology, tells Upworthy that flexibility—specifically being open to a relationship being dynamic and shifting—is a key personality trait of those who maintain long-term friendships. “Twenty years is a long time—you’ll probably be a different person than you were at the beginning of the relationship, and so will the other person,” he explains. “They’ll change at different rates than you do and have different events that come along in their lives, and that will make it inconvenient or challenging.” Personality trait No. 2: They value depth and commitment “This means they are not looking for something easy; they are looking for something mutually sustainable,” Blythe Landry , LCSW, M.Ed., founder of Grief to Purpose, tells Upworthy. “Long-term friendships require the same willingness to invest time, mutual support, and deep vulnerability that romantic relationships do. If you value these things, that is a good starting point for long-term friendship success.” Personality trait No. 3: They value stability over novelty The concept of “novelty,” or something being shiny and new, typically doesn’t hold as much value to those with long-term friendships. “Some people deeply value being known by people who have seen them through many seasons of life. They’ve watched you grow and struggle and change,” Dr. Holovatyk explains. “There’s a grounding, nervous-system-level comfort in being with someone who knows your history and doesn’t need the backstory. People who keep friends for decades tend to prize that depth over the excitement of constantly meeting someone new.” Personality trait No. 4: They are resilient A certain level of grit and resilience is necessary for friendships to last 20 years. “Being able to continue through the relationship when things are challenging, and continue putting in that effort even if it’s not always fun and easy,” Glickman says. Personality trait No. 5: They are comfortable with conflict People with 20-year friendships are okay with not expecting themselves or others to always show up the way they want them to. “Long-term friendships require both parties to recognize that nobody is perfect, that sometimes the connection will be more vital than others, and that both people will make mistakes,” Landry explains. “Willingness to work through the hard times is a core component of long-term relationships of all kinds.” Personality trait No. 6: They have the capacity to assume goodwill “This means that the person recognizes the vicissitudes of life will be what they are, and that someone needing to focus more on their kids or aging parents for sometimes years at a time doesn’t mean the love is gone; it means the availability has temporarily changed,” says Landry. In other words, although it may feel uncomfortable, they can look at the bigger picture. “People who assume goodwill and know that most people are doing the best they can are able to make room for long-term friendships, all of which ebb and flow in connection over time,” she shares. Sturnick also adds, “The friends who last don’t track who called last. They trust it evens out over decades, not weeks.” The post Psychologists explain 6 traits of people who have kept friends for 20 years appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Οι συγκεντρώσεις των PFOS και PFOA, των δύο πιο τοξικών για πάντα χημικών ουσιών, έχουν μειωθεί κατά 30 τοις εκατό και 29 τοις εκατό στα ποτάμια της Αγγλίας τα τελευταία 10 χρόνια, σύμφωνα με νέα στοιχεία της Υπηρεσίας Περιβάλλοντος (EA). Στα ψάρια του γλυκού νερού, τα επίπεδα μειώνονται κατά 49%. Ο οργανισμός αποδίδει την πτώση σε περιορισμό…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA, the two most toxic forever chemicals , have fallen by 30 percent and 29 percent in England’s rivers over the past 10 years, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). In freshwater fish , levels are down 49 percent. The agency attributes the decline to restrictions that removed both compounds from most products, which makes the data one of the clearer measures yet of what a chemical ban does to a river system over time. Two forever chemicals, two bans, one decade of data PFOS and PFOA PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, were first developed in the U.S. in the 1930s. Manufacturers adopted them for their resistance to oil, water, and heat, and they ended up in nonstick pans, firefighting foam, and electrical components. The same chemical stability means they take a very long time to break down, which earned them the label forever chemicals. PFOS and PFOA were among the earliest compounds in the family. About 20 years ago, researchers began linking them to tissue damage in animals and to higher rates of certain serious illnesses in people, including testicular cancer . The UK all but banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. Results from the latest Environment Agency figures The new data, published by the EA this month, covers 10 years of monitoring. Both chemicals declined by nearly a third in river water, while the near-halving in fish points to less of the compounds moving up the food chain. Dr. David Megson, a reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, welcomed the trend. “It’s brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years,” he said. Lower concentrations, same total load Where forever chemicals go after a ban The EA report attaches a significant caveat to its own numbers. Because PFOS and PFOA break down so slowly, the total quantity in the environment has likely not changed much. Concentrations in rivers have dropped because the chemicals have been diluted and carried downstream into the sea. A ban stops new inputs, but it does not remove what is already circulating. Very few methods can destroy PFAS permanently. High-temperature incineration is one of them, and England currently has only two facilities suited to the job. Making polluters pay Megson sees the monitoring record as a starting point for accountability. “There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused,” he said. Regulating PFAS as a group 15,000 compounds, 200 in common use PFOS and PFOA are two of an estimated 15,000 PFAS, of which around 200 are in frequent use. The EA said that “uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS” and that its findings reinforce the case for regulating the chemicals as a class instead of one at a time. The chemicals industry has long resisted a group approach, arguing that evidence of toxicity for most other PFAS is limited or absent and that some have essential applications, including in life-saving medical equipment. Wider monitoring The agency now tests regularly for 60 additional PFAS to map contamination across England, and the government announced earlier this month that it will begin measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies. Taken together with the river data, those programs will show whether the pattern seen with PFOS and PFOA holds for other compounds once restrictions arrive: a slow but steady fall in water and wildlife, with the legacy load still to be dealt with downstream. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It’s 6 p.m. on a Friday, and the dinner you booked two weeks ago is in an hour. Back then it sounded like the perfect plan. But now your couch has never looked softer, your sweatpants feel like a hug, and your thumb is hovering over a message that starts with “So sorry, something came up…” Nothing came up, of course. You just don’t want to go anymore, and you can’t quite explain why. If that sounds familiar, you have plenty of company. According to the Survey Center on American Life , 55 percent of Gen Z adults say they feel relief when plans fall through. In the U.K., research from the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that 68 percent of people under 34 have bailed on plans, and one in 10 do it “very often.” There’s a name for that late-afternoon dread, and once you can name it, it gets a lot easier to put your shoes on anyway. What anticipatory anxiety feels like The doorway as a dividing line Mindy DeSeta , a licensed mental health counselor, calls it anticipatory anxiety. “It’s the stress we feel before something happens,” she says. Part of the pull comes from home itself, which is familiar and predictable in a way a crowded restaurant isn’t. “Walking through the doorway is the visual trigger that separates your safe space from the unknown,” DeSeta said. It’s the same jittery feeling you might have had before a school recital or a big presentation at work, just pointed at something that’s supposed to be fun. Why the dread rarely matches the night Think back to the last time you went out despite wanting to cancel. Chances are, an hour in, you were laughing at something and had forgotten all about the couch. DeSeta has seen that pattern again and again. “In most cases, the anticipation anxiety is often worse than the event itself. Don’t allow the jitters to deter you!” she said. What canceling plans costs your friends When everyone bails, everyone feels it Canceling feels harmless in the moment, and sometimes it’s the right call. But when it becomes a habit for a whole generation, someone is always on the other end of that text. Rachel Schleider, a 23-year-old social strategist said her birthday has become a source of stress for exactly this reason. “I literally dread making plans for my birthday every year because I know people are going to cancel the day before,” she said. She thinks the culture around flaking has swung too far. “We’ve kind of taken it too far and now people are way too comfortable bowing out,” Schleider said. How to manage anticipatory anxiety before a plan Name it, then don’t negotiate with it DeSeta’s first suggestion is to call the feeling what it is. Once you recognize the dread as anticipatory anxiety, you can remind yourself that the feeling isn’t an instruction. Feeling uneasy about going is a different thing from having a reason not to go. Breathe, and look at what the nerves are telling you A few slow, deep breaths can take the edge off the physical side of it, the tight chest and the restless hands. It also helps to flip the meaning of the nerves around. Feeling jittery about seeing someone usually means the plan matters to you, which is a reason to show up instead of a reason to stay home. Set an alarm and let the routine carry you DeSeta’s most practical trick happens before the dread has a chance to build: set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, get in the shower and get dressed without debating it. By the time your hair is dry, you’re most of the way out the door. None of this means you should drag yourself out when you’re sick or running on empty. Rest is a valid reason to cancel. But if the only thing standing between you and your friends is that familiar pre-plan heaviness, it might help to picture the walk home afterward, a little tired and full and glad you went, and let that version of the evening make the decision for you. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Florence Pugh recently reminded fans that bodies change , and not always as a result of needles and knives . More and more celebrities are speaking openly about the “work” they’ve had done, be it with plastic surgery, GLP-1s, or other cosmetic enhancements. As with most things, this transparency has brought both good and bad. On the one hand, it’s made the topic much less taboo and shrouded in mystery. On the other hand, the influx of social media analyses about celebrity appearance changes, whether from fans, stylists, beauty bloggers, or plastic surgeons trying to gain clout, might be affecting our discernment. This was the point actress Florence Pugh was making following recent speculation that she secretly underwent a major cosmetic procedure. In a video posted online, photos of Pugh from recent years were compared to one of her looks at Sunday’s Governor Awards, where her chin appeared more “defined.” Pugh was then dubbed yet another “fallen victim to Hollywood’s war on round faces.” View this post on Instagram Pugh had a very different explanation Pugh laid it out plainly in the comments section, writing, “Guys. I turned 30. I’m a woman. [Bodies] and faces change. It’s not that deep, the fact that people can’t even tell between what’s aging and what’s surgery is disturbing.” She then gave the reality check that “Sadly puppy fluff doesn’t last forever.” In a subsequent Instagram post , Pugh elaborated that, rather than the effects of Ozempic or plastic surgery, her change in appearance was purely the result of growing older and learning to take better care of herself. “Here’s the truth, I turned 30 and my New Year’s Resolution was to change my relationship with alcohol, and to be able to do at least one pull-up in the gym. It’s funny to see you all use reference images from times when I was really mentally unhappy and abusing my body and put it next to the image from the governor’s ball the other night where I am happy and respecting my body. “For the first time in my ENTIRE career, I had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily. I’ve WANTED to move my body and not take it for granted. Guess how much weight I’ve lost in all that. 2 pounds. Because the thing that’s most important to me and my trainer is muscle. “I’m looking after myself, and that’s literally it.” View this post on Instagram She has spent years being scrutinized for her appearance That might be the biggest takeaway of all. Pugh isn’t arguing that there’s anything wrong with cosmetic procedures. She’s pointing out how strange it is that people saw a woman who had recently turned 30 looking different from how she did years earlier and immediately started searching for an explanation involving surgery or medication. Pugh also noted that her appearance has been a public conversation for her entire professional life, from being “subjected to fat shaming” and told she “SHOULD go on Ozempic” to now being accused of using it. That history makes her response particularly pointed. She has been told her body needed to change, and now that it has changed naturally, people assume she must have done something to make it happen. Now she is asking people to consider the possibility that sometimes a different-looking face is simply a different-looking face. Social media makes it easy to look for a dramatic explanation There’s nothing inherently wrong with wanting to understand the beauty standards surrounding celebrities, or with having conversations about the ways Hollywood influences what people consider attractive. There is also nothing wrong with someone choosing cosmetic work if that’s what they want. But there is a difference between examining those larger pressures and deciding that an individual woman’s face is a mystery that the internet needs to solve. Social media has made that kind of speculation remarkably easy. A weight change can suddenly become unfounded evidence of a medication. A different jawline can become “proof” of surgery. A new hairstyle or makeup technique can be mistaken for a miraculous “transformation.” Sometimes, though, the explanation is much less dramatic: people change. Pugh’s reminder applies far beyond Hollywood View this post on Instagram Pugh’s request is fairly straightforward: let people change without the feedback. Let them get stronger, lose weight, gain weight, change their hair, change their makeup, or just wake up one morning and look different than they did five years ago. That applies to celebrities, but also to everyone scrolling through those photos and comparing them with their own. If you’re looking at an old photo of yourself and thinking you don’t look like that anymore, well, congratulations. You’re alive. As Pugh put it, “Puppy fluff doesn’t last forever.” Thankfully, it doesn’t need to. The post Florence Pugh posted a fantastic reality check about aging after plastic surgery rumors appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο Ρομπ Λόου μιλάει για την παιδική του ηλικία, τη νοσταλγία του Gen X και τις δεύτερες ευκαιρίες

Σε σκηνοθεσία Chris Smith, η ταινία εξερευνά τους πιο εμβληματικούς ρόλους του Lowe, συμπεριλαμβανομένου του ασυνήθιστου συντρόφου του…
items.descriptionOriginal: Rob Lowe helped define Gen X through his many iconic TV and film roles. Now, The West Wing star is sharing never-before-seen footage and stories from his upbringing and career in the new Netflix documentary Rob Lowe: The Outsider , premiering November 24. Directed by Chris Smith, the film explores Lowe’s most iconic roles, including his breakout performance in The Outsiders , which inspired the documentary’s title. It also features personal footage from his childhood in Dayton, Ohio; his family’s move to Malibu, California; and additional home videos shot by Lowe on his camcorder. “Those things [camcorders] are back,” Lowe tells Upworthy, referring to the analog technology. He sat down with Upworthy to discuss his new documentary, parenting, the Gen X things he’s still nostalgic for, and how he’s literally letting go of some of them through “Modern Masters: The Rob Lowe Collection,” a live auction hosted by Julien’s Auctions on December 16 featuring nearly 150 items from the actor’s personal collection. Lowe says he was always an Outsider Throughout the documentary, Lowe explores a recurring theme in his life: the desire to be “seen.” He describes his desperate attempts to get his parents, Barbara Lynn Hepler and Charles “Chuck” Davis Lowe, to see him and his younger brother, Chad Lowe. His parents divorced when he was just 4 years old. “The most fundamental human trait is wanting to be seen for who one is—and it’s surprisingly rare,” he says. “And if you get to be famous, you have the added jarring element that everybody thinks they know you, but they don’t really.” He then opens up about the challenges of finding fame after his breakout role on the 1979 ABC sitcom A New Kind of Family . “You have to find your own authenticity, know who you are—before anybody else can really know you,” he says. Among Lowe’s closest friends and co-stars are Gwyneth Paltrow, Demi Moore, Mike Myers, and his The Outsiders co-star C. Thomas Howell. “I just continue to be grateful and to realize how blessed I am that I have these kinds of opportunities, and that this documentary continues the four decades of relationships that I’ve had with people who I may never meet who are watching what I do,” Lowe says. Rob Lowe and Sheryl Berkoff. Photo Courtesy: Netflix On marriage and lasting relationships Lowe married Sheryl Berkoff on July 22, 1991. The couple first met in 1983 but reconnected when Berkoff worked as his makeup artist on the 1989 film Bad Influence . “She saw me in a way when I met her that no one else [in my dating life] had yet,” Lowe says. “And I don’t know if that was because she was a makeup artist and it was literally her job—but it wasn’t just that. I don’t know if it’s kismet, if it’s chemistry—when you are seen authentically, you know it. And she did.” Lowe has learned the value of repairing relationships and working through conflicts in his own life. And when asked about the growing cultural trend of “going no contact” and “cutoff culture,” he has some thoughts. “So I actually have a pretty strong opinion on this,” he says. “We live in a society that is so obsessed with boundaries, which is obviously great. People running roughshod over your boundaries is a horrible, horrible thing. But as we do as a society, we always overcorrect. We always swing way past normal to the other side.” Reflecting on divorce, Lowe explains, “When my mom was growing up, nobody got divorced. It was a bad mark on your character. And then in her generation, everybody got divorced. And I think now when people talk about marriage or relationships with their parents, we’re so obsessed with getting our needs met.” And when those needs aren’t met, Lowe turns to a travel analogy to explain what can happen: “I feel like we treat people like passengers on a plane. The very first thing that they tell them is how to get the hell out. Here are the exits,” he explains. “It’s all about teaching people how to leave and nobody teaching people about how to stay. I would like to see all of us fight to stay in relationships unless they’re so egregious, so unspeakably, clearly unhealthy. Because my guess is most of them aren’t. And it’s very easy to run. But it’s more fulfilling to stay.” What Lowe has learned about parenting Lowe and Berkoff are proud parents to two sons, Matthew, 33, and John, 31. In The Outsider , Lowe reflects on how becoming a father changed him. “When I met my wife, and it was time for me to start raising a family, I was really ready for that. I had no illusions about that. I was done,” he says. “I had gone to every restaurant. I’d gone to every nightclub. I’d been on every date. I had done it and more and loved every minute of it.” Lowe wanted to be a present father so his sons would feel “seen.” At the time, that meant accepting a role on a new political drama called The West Wing , which required him to take a 50% pay cut but allowed him to spend more time with his family. “I loved serving hot lunch every Wednesday to the kids at the school. I loved coaching Little League. I loved working on homework. I loved it. I miss it.” View this post on Instagram On recovery and finding stillness Lowe’s journey to sobriety is a highlight of The Outsider . In the film, he recalls feeling “tired” after years of “chase and chase,” noting that he was “25, but felt 45.” He got sober on May 10, 1990, at age 26. For Lowe, one of the greatest gifts of recovery has been overcoming FOMO (fear of missing out). “I was always convinced there was a better, more exclusive, cooler thing going on. And what recovery taught me was that I don’t need any of that. I’m good in my own company,” he says. “I’m happy to sit with the dogs and look at the stars or read a book or wander around. I don’t need that feedback, that buzz, that adrenaline. I’m not a hermit. But I could live remotely. I could live away from everybody, and I could be fine. And I might even do that someday. And that would have been unthinkable in the days when I was like, ‘What are we doing? What’s happening? Let’s go! Let’s kill it! Let’s crush it!’ I think it’s really important to be able to be still with yourself and be okay with it.” On Gen X nostalgia Lowe was born on March 17, 1964, technically making him a Baby Boomer (those born between 1946 and 1964). But he identifies more with Gen X. “I am nostalgic for so many things,” he says. “I am so lucky that I am the age I am and lived when I lived, because I believe that I grew up in the best era that has ever been on planet Earth.” He adds that he “hit the lottery” alongside those “who had their childhood years in the ’70s, their teenage years and 20s in the ’80s.” Lowe continues, “[We] hit the chronological lottery. And it’s impossible to describe what it was like.” There are plenty of things from that era he still misses. “I miss waking up as a kid and in the summer, being barefoot all day, running around the neighborhood,” he says. “Your parents didn’t know where you were. And then when the streetlights came on, that’s when you went home, and you could do whatever. You were wild, and nobody cared. And it was great.” And that includes some of his favorite childhood treats. “I’m a Midwestern kid who grew up in the middle class. So I miss Hostess Ho-Hos and Hostess Fruit Pies. I love those things. And God knows what was in them, but nothing tastes the way it used to taste,” he says. “I miss my ’70s junk food and my ’70s bubble gum, Bazooka—the one that came in the long [the Big Buddy]. And every once in a while you’ll find a candy store that has it and it’s super sick.” Although his camcorder days are behind him, there’s another camera he still misses: the Polaroid. “I miss the old Polaroid. Just the [makes clicking sound]. That was so satisfying. And then, of course, ‘shake it, shake it, shake it like a Polaroid picture.’ I miss those,” Lowe says. While Lowe finds joy in the things of the past, he continues to look toward the future and relish more moments of stillness. “What’s the cliché, that ‘there’s a season for all things’? When you’re younger, you want to take a big bite out of life. And I still am a guy who [when] given an opportunity, I’m taking it,” he says. “I’m gonna go to that prize fight. I’m gonna go on that trip. I’m gonna go to that dinner. I’m gonna meet that person. I’m gonna extend myself. I take advantage of the opportunities I’m given. But on the other side of it, given the choice—[I’m choosing my] dogs in the backyard, fire pit, and sunset on the mountains. That would not have been my ideal night when I was younger—as it should be.” The post Rob Lowe gets intimate about his childhood, Gen X nostalgia, and second chances appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Although vegans generally have a healthy gut microbiome, they may be at risk of having lower gut bacterial diversity than omnivores, according to the author of a new study. The gut is home to billions of microorganisms. It is a complex ecosystem that regulates many of the body’s functions and helps keep us healthy—when it is in balance. Our diet influences this ecosystem. But what role does it play whether a person is vegan or omnivorous? In a new study, researchers from the University of Copenhagen examined this question by closely investigating the gut microbiome of 75 vegans and 75 omnivorous Danes. The researchers initially expected the vegan group to have the healthiest gut microbiome across all parameters. However, they found one notable weakness: gut bacterial diversity was, on average, lower among vegans than among omnivores. “This came as a major surprise. Because vegans eat only plant-based foods and therefore consume large amounts of dietary fiber and other health-promoting plant compounds that stimulate the gut microbiome, we expected the vegan group to have greater bacterial diversity than the omnivores. But that was not the case,” says Oluf Borbye Pedersen, professor at the Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Basic Metabolic Research. He adds: “The study suggests that the lower average diversity of gut bacteria among vegans may be linked to their lower protein intake. Among vegans, 12% of dietary energy came from protein, compared with 17% among omnivores. However, the vegans who consumed the most protein had biodiversity levels comparable to those of the omnivores. Protein may therefore be an overlooked factor for a diverse gut microbiome among vegans.” The researchers are interested in gut health because it is crucial to overall health. In this context, having a diversity of bacteria is considered beneficial. “Our gut is an enormously complex ecosystem. It can be compared to a rainforest, which functions best when it houses as many different species as possible. The same applies to our internal microbial ecosystem. It should ideally be as diverse as possible,” says Pedersen. “High biodiversity is a sign of a healthy and resilient gut microbiome. And a healthy microbiome is not only essential for digestion and metabolism, it also plays an important role in immune function and brain health.” To understand the differences between vegans and omnivores, the researchers analyzed stool, blood, and urine samples. They then mapped the bacteria and viruses in the gut as well as signaling molecules in the body. “Apart from the reduced diversity of gut bacteria, we found that the vegans had a health-promoting gut microbiome,” says Pedersen. The vegans consumed more carbohydrates and dietary fiber and, on average, less protein and fat than the omnivores. They also had higher levels of several bacterial species capable of breaking down dietary fiber, along with a greater prevalence of the organism Blastocystis, which has been associated with lower blood pressure. The vegans also had lower blood glucose and cholesterol levels. Compared with the omnivores, they also had fewer inflammatory markers in the body. The researchers emphasize that the study is relatively small and observational comparing existing dietary patterns. The results may therefore point to associations, but they cannot establish whether specific dietary habits directly cause changes in the gut microbiome or to gut health, for example whether protein intake directly causes changes in gut biodiversity. As such, Pedersen cannot make dietary recommendations based on the new study. However, he says the findings support the importance of ensuring adequate nutrition, regardless of dietary preference: “Vegans in particular should consider whether they are getting enough protein in their diet, since they do not obtain it from meat, eggs, or dairy products. Good vegan sources of protein include beans, lentils, hemp seeds, chia seeds, quinoa, almonds, and nuts.” The research appears in Microbiome . Source: University of Copenhagen The post Vegan gut bacteria discovery surprises researchers appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Antibodies that coat the lining of your gut may be playing an important role in preventing colon cancer from developing, scientists have discovered. Mice that lack a specific class of antibodies, called immunoglobulin A (IgA), develop more than twice as many colon tumors as usual, the team reports in Nature . The study also explained why: When the antibodies bind to the cells lining the inside of the gut, it keeps those cells from dividing too quickly—which could lead to cancer. When the researchers gave IgA-deficient mice oral doses of the antibodies, they no longer had a higher risk of developing tumors. “One intriguing aspect of this work is that it shows how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer,” says senior author Daniel Mucida, head of Rockefeller University’s Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. “Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?” The discovery illuminates why people with IgA deficiency—who have few or none of these antibodies—are at a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer but also could shed light on other aspects of the complex interplay between the gut microbes, immune system, and cancer—even in otherwise healthy people. Scientists and clinicians have long known that the gut has high levels of IgA. Unlike many antibodies that are highly specific for one pathogen at a time, IgA is a broad-acting first line of defense in the immune system. A single IgA molecule can bind to a wide range of gut bacteria—as well as some healthy human cells—but researchers had long wondered why there were such high levels of IgA in the digestive system. Mucida and his colleagues study how the intestine strikes a balance between protecting the body against invading pathogens and absorbing the nutrients the body needs. In the past, for instance, the lab has discovered the role that gut immune cells play in food intolerances and allergies. In the new work, former Rockefeller postdoctoral fellow Gregory Donaldson—now an assistant professor at UCLA—wanted to tease out exactly how IgA antibodies interact with gut bacteria, and whether that could be relevant to colon cancer. “We know these antibodies bind bacteria and by doing so can shape the microbiome,” he says. “And because IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the US, is linked to colorectal cancer, I wondered whether these interactions might be relevant to the disease.” Donaldson began by studying IgA-deficient mice that were raised alongside normal mice, ensuring that they were exposed to the same germs and food. The mice without IgA developed more colorectal cancers than those who had IgA—echoing what was already known to occur in humans. “We found this was true for several different kinds of models of colon cancer, so that was a really convincing effect,” says Donaldson. Moreover, giving these mice an oral treatment of IgA molecules eliminated the increased risk of cancer. Mucida, Donaldson, and the rest of their group zoomed in to the cells lining the gut, called epithelial cells—where colon cancers first form—to see how they were different in the mice lacking IgA. They discovered that changes in gene expression included ones related to cell division, or proliferation, and that these changes came before any tumors ever emerged. “We assumed there must be some sort of receptor on the epithelial cells that was mediating this,” Donaldson says. Second author Gabriella Lima dos Reis, a graduate student in Gabriel Victora’s lab, homed in on one receptor that is found on the surface of epithelial cells and that IgA can bind to. Called DMBT1, it had already been linked in multiple ways to some cancers, but its exact role in colon cancer was unclear. The team went on to show that DMBT1, in the presence of gut bacteria, acts as a gas pedal for cell proliferation. But IgA, when it binds to DMBT1, acts as a brake. If IgA is completely absent, DMBT1 signaling is unrestrained, letting gut epithelial cells divide more than usual and form tumors. But without gut bacteria, without DMBT1 signaling, or with normal IgA levels, the epithelial cells are kept in check. “If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function—responding to bacteria by producing new cells—can keep dividing, leading to cancer,” Mucida says. “We think this homeostatic effect is IgA’s main function. This was a big surprise.” By establishing DMBT1’s natural function in epithelial cells for the first time, the findings may lay the groundwork for new interventions to reduce colon cancer risk. “Based on the mechanism we discovered, perhaps we could influence epithelial cells to be less likely to develop into a tumor,” Mucida says. “We know, for example, that having polyps increases your chances of getting colon cancer, so we think that there could be an opportunity to target this pathway after polyps are removed. Right now, there are no interventions available at that point.” “What is potentially even more exciting is that there is evidence that individual species of bacteria can have really specific effects on epithelial cells as well,” Donaldson notes. “A lot of research has focused on bacteria that induce tumors or can exacerbate their growth, but we have some evidence that there are bacteria that could do the opposite, just as IgA does. To that end, perhaps we could develop a probiotic supplement that induces a protective IgA response. This is all very speculative, but it’s one direction that we could look toward in the future.” Mucida adds, “Overall, there is a lot more to learn about how the dance between bacteria, antibodies, and epithelial cells in the gut works to maintain health.” Source: Rockefeller University The post Gut antibodies may help protect against colon cancer appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Types of Cycling Explained for Eco Riders and Race Followers Reading Time: 4 minutes From Daily Rides to Pro Races, Cycling Comes In Many Forms. Here’s a Simple Guide to Each One What Do You Mean by Cycling? Everyday Riding for a Greener Life The cost of gas and vehicle repairs and maintenance has many people looking at cycling as an alternative way to get around, but what do you mean by cycling exactly? Depending on where you’re cycling and your purpose for doing the activity, there are different types of cycling available for you. Some people are just looking to get places on main streets, while others are more adventurous and want to explore with off-road cycling. There are many different types of cycling , so let’s take a closer look at what the best might be for you. The Best Bicycle for Beginners So you think you want to give cycling a try. But what is the best bicycle for beginners ? As we already talked about, it really depends on the type of cycling you’re wanting to get into. There are many different types of cycling, and your equipment needs to fit the type that you are doing. Anyone who bikes regularly knows that each has its own needs, so your equipment needs to match where and how you’re going to be cycling. Different Types of Cycling: Road, Track, Mountain and More So what are the different types of cycling? There are many, as the sport has few limits on how you decide to approach it. For getting places and more relaxing rides, there is road cycling. This occurs – as the name implies – on roads, so there isn’t much terrain to worry about. The bike for road cycling is more sleek and aerodynamic, allowing for smoother rides on the smoother terrain that is being used. This leads to track cycling, where speed is more of a concern. The cycle and the attire of the cyclist are made for less wind resistance and greater speeds. Mountain biking comes with less predictable terrain, so the cycle itself must have more of a suspension system and wider tires to help the cyclist deal with the different obstacles that come up. There is less of a need for being aerodynamic with the cycle and the attire, since this type of cycling is more focused on getting through off-road trails. Another of the types of cycling is gravel cycling, which is a bit of a cross between mountain biking and road cycling. As you might guess, this type is on gravel trails, which brings fewer obstacles and a bit more stability on trails than mountain biking. The type of bike for this is a cross between mountain biking and road cycling, with wider tires but less suspension. A growing form of cycling is e-biking, which can be applied to almost any form of cycling. This is not a motorcycle or moped, as the cyclist still has to be doing work. The motor and battery on an e-bike assist when needed to make for longer rides and easier times for cyclists when they face obstacles like a steep climb. There are also racing forms of cycling, whether on streets like the Tour de France or over ramps and jumps in BMX racing. Types of Bicycle Racing in the Olympics When it comes to racing, the top venue for cycling is the Olympics. There are five different disciplines that are held in the Summer Olympic Games. Road cycling is done on outdoor courses with a mass-start road race. Also on outdoor courses is mountain bike racing, with rougher natural terrain, steep climbs, and obstacles. One of the more popular types of bicycle racing at the Olympics is track cycling, which is held on a banked oval track using fixed-gear bicycles with no brakes. There are multiple different events within this form of cycling, including team pursuit and sprints. There are two types of BMX racing in the Olympics as well. BMX racing is held on dirt tracks with as many as eight cyclists running the course filled with jumps and banked turns at a time. There is also BMX freestyle, which is a judged competition as riders perform tricks in a one-minute run on a park course. Bicycle Racing Categories Every Fan Should Know One of the most popular bicycle racing categories , or sporting events, in the world is the Tour de France, which is a stage race over multiple days that tests a cyclist’s endurance and strategy. Cyclists have stages that they complete each day, with the Tour de France having 21 stages over three weeks. It has made stars out of past winners like Greg LeMond and Lance Armstrong, and is also a big betting event for fans. Speaking of betting, you can see BetUS Sportsbook odds to win the 2027 Tour de France. There is also a form of racing called criteriums, which are shorter races in both distance and time but are just as spectator- and betting-friendly. These are often on street courses like auto racing, with the cyclists going around a track and past spectators. You can also find road races that are held over street courses for longer distances. These can be held with a mass start (everyone all at once), or in individual time trials where cyclists start in staggered intervals. FAQs What are the different types of cycling? There are many different types of cycling, from road cycling, mountain biking, gravel cycling, BMX cycling, e-biking, and track cycling. Which type of cycle is best for racing? The type of cycle needed for racing depends on the type of racing being done. Track or road cycling is different from off-road or BMX racing. Each type of racing requires a different kind of bicycle. How is a gravel bike different from a mountain bike? A gravel bike is made to be a combination of a mountain bike and a road bike, so it has the look of a road bike but the features of a mountain bike as well. They have wider tires and a more relaxed frame to give more versatility than a straight mountain bike. The post Types of Cycling Explained for Eco Riders and Race Followers appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Energy Behind Online Casinos: Can Digital Gaming Run on Cleaner Power? Reading Time: 3 minutes Every spin, stream, and click runs on electricity somewhere. Here’s where that energy goes, and how cleaner power is changing the picture. Energy consumption of online gaming isn’t at the forefront of players’ minds when they log in and get ready for a playing session. It is on the mind of those who are behind the scenes and running these sites and platforms. How Much Energy Does Online Gaming Use? Online casino energy consumption is a huge factor. Every game on a screen sits on a server working away in a data center. That would be every game that is played; add in live streams and shows that are hosted, and other essentials to get the performance that is expected, and it turns into an electricity spending spree. The Carbon Footprint of Online Gaming The carbon footprint depends on where the electricity comes from. And it is definitely a source where online gaming businesses are trying to find ways to lower the costs of operation. The more streamlined a business, the better it can serve its customers … and its operations. Research shows gaming represents $5 billion per year in energy expenditures across the United States, with carbon-dioxide emissions equivalent to that of 85 million refrigerators or over 5 million cars. According to the International Energy Agency, data centers globally consumed approximately 460 terawatt-hours in 2022, accounting for nearly 2% of total electricity demand. That was almost five years ago. Imagine what the number is now as more and more people turn to online gaming for entertainment. Rising computing power, improved graphics quality, higher-resolution displays, and streaming delivery have rendered computer gaming an increasingly energy-intensive activity. Green data centers are a big piece of the equation in this business, as sites try to find ways to be more economical and prudent. Green Data Centers and the Shift to Cleaner Power There are options, for sure. An eco-friendly online casino operation understands that wind and solar are powering more of the internet. Green data centers rely on renewables, smarter cooling, and efficient servers. The cooler the center, the less energy is drained. Cooling methods for servers can account for 40% of the total energy consumption, hence the carbon footprint of online gaming. And, with the rising electricity demand worldwide … Small Changes That Make Gaming Greener Not every fix needs a power plant. Efficient software, lighter websites, and energy-saving devices can help the cause. Additionally, liquid cooling technology and smart temperature management systems can reduce energy usage dramatically, according to Uptime Institute research. What an Eco-Friendly Online Casino Looks Like Picture a platform built to be lean, fast, and efficient. Leading online gambling operators are increasingly adopting sustainable data centers and green data center practices, including: Implementation of energy-efficient servers and hardware, use of renewable energy sources for power, advanced heat recycling systems, AI-powered optimization of server loads, and geographic positioning in naturally cool climates. This all moves in the direction of sustainable online gaming, such as for those who play any of the casino games available at BetUS , for example. It’s good to know that modern casinos like BetUS Casino offer quick, digital payouts with less waste. The less waste, the less energy, and the greater the feasibility of the business. Heading in the direction of eco-friendly server infrastructure is needed for sustainable online gambling operations. FAQs Are online casinos greener than land-based casinos? Online casinos are most likely greener than land-based casinos, sending out fewer emissions than brick-and-mortar venues. Can data centers run entirely on renewable energy? There are data centers that run on renewable energy. It remains a challenging task that many are tackling and hoping to improve upon. How much electricity does an hour of online gaming use?
