items.descriptionOriginal: Literacy, the ability to read, used to be a rare thing. Only 200 years ago, as few as 12% of people around the world could read at a basic level. Today, that global number is around 87% , and in the United States, 99% of adults can read at least at around a fifth-grade level. In the long arc of history, that’s incredible progress. But there’s a catch. In the U.S., about 28% of adults are functionally illiterate, which means they “face significant challenges when trying to comprehend or use written information in practical contexts,” according to Babbel . In other words, there’s a huge difference between being able to read words and understand sentences and being truly, functionally literate . Mental health coach explains the massive literacy gap Dr. Shanté Holley, an English professor and popular, trauma-informed mental health coach on social media, recently did a deep dive into this topic on her YouTube channel . “There are so many people that just don’t understand nuance, satire, entendre, or irony,” she says in a video. “Illiteracy cripples your ability to read the world and the room. … The difference between people who regularly wrestle with complex ideas vs. people who primarily consume clickbait content is vast.” Reading comprehension is essential. Photo credit: Canva She goes on to explain that literacy goes far beyond just being able to read. It’s about being able to understand what you’re reading. In 2026, access to information is almost unlimited. The early days of the printing press, when books and printed text were luxuries for the wealthy, are long gone. Now it’s the ability to interpret that information that is the true superpower. Have you ever seen a thing online and immediately scrolled to the comments in order to figure out how you should feel about it? Most of us are guilty, and Holley calls this “outsourcing your intellect.” Even Google’s AI Overviews take answers that were nearly instant to begin with and save us the trouble of having to even read the original source at all. This outsourcing can have worse effects than just deciding whether to like a social media post. “In real actual life, think of when you’re applying for a mortgage, or there’s a health directive at the hospital, when you need to interpret certain clauses in insurance policies, when there are tax changes in your community … and you don’t understand, then you are at the mercy of someone else reading that situation for you,” Holley says. She says there’s a growing number of people who can only recite talking points developed by others because they lack the ability (or the effort) to analyze things on their own. And when these people step into voting booths, it becomes dangerous for everyone. But not only that, mismatches in literacy can erode friendships, marriages, and more. It’s a brilliant plea, and well worth watching in its entirety: Literacy is a massive driver of success and happiness Enough doom and gloom. In the video, Holley says that the “elite,” like billionaires and tech CEOs, barely use, and keep their kids far away from, the very social media and technology they’ve created. Famously, Steve Jobs and Bill Gates insisted on low-tech households for their children. Instead, they study power, politics, art, and history. Their kids receive classical educations at the best schools. And while Holley says that literacy does not require a formal education or a fancy Ivy League degree, the point remains that the people in charge know far too well that true knowledge and critical thinking do not come from bite-sized content on the internet. Everyone knows that reading is good for you. But not everyone knows just how outrageously good having strong literacy skills really is. Mental health Poor literacy has been strongly associated with negative mental health outcomes like anxiety and depression. Strong literacy skills give people increased self-confidence, self-worth, and a sense of agency in the world, which contributes to greater resilience. Wealth Our income is strongly related to our literacy. Literacy Texas writes, “Nationwide, low-literate adults struggle to earn a living wage, participate in the democratic process, and manage their family’s health and finances simply because they lack the ability to read, write and comprehend.” Strong critical thinkers who excel at writing and reading have a leg up financially in more ways than you can count. Longevity Researchers at Yale University recently discovered that “people who read books regularly had a 20% lower risk of dying over the next 12 years” compared to less literate peers. Literacy and reading comprehension skills can degrade if not used. But they can also be rebuilt and improved with practice. Simple ways to build your literacy Here’s what Holley suggests to improve your literacy in just a few minutes per day: Read one longform article per day She recommends the AP, Reuters, The Atlantic , or The New Yorker to start. “Not to agree with it, but to practice reading something that has your full attention,” she says. Read one nonfiction book per quarter In 2025, a YouGov poll found that 40% of Americans read no books at all, while a Pew Research Center survey put the figure at 25%. Now, there are a lot of ways to access information and knowledge besides books, but the effect is only compounded by time spent on social media. Holley suggests nonfiction to grow your knowledge base, but fiction is just as effective for developing your mastery of context, subtext, irony, and language. Replace 20 minutes of scrolling time with a lecture or documentary Literacy is not just about reading; it’s about synthesizing information. Documentaries or TED Talks on YouTube are fair game for growing your knowledge base if they’re challenging you to process new ideas. Similarly, audiobooks are just as effective as print for comprehension. “The future belongs to the people who can make sense of the world, not just consume it,” Holley writes in the video’s caption. A small trade with a big payoff None of Holley’s suggestions require overhauling your entire life. A longform article here, a documentary there, a few pages of a book before bed instead of another scroll through the feed. The shift is small enough to actually stick, which is exactly the point. It’s amazing to think about the incredible ripple effect that can happen when we trade just a few minutes per day of scrolling for reading. That ripple effect isn’t abstract. It shows up in how confidently you read a contract, how clearly you spot a bad-faith argument online, how well you understand your own health directive at the hospital. Literacy was never really about finishing books. It’s about staying capable of thinking for yourself in a world that would rather do the thinking for you. This article originally appeared in June. It has been updated. The post English professor explains why happy, successful people have one thing in common: true literacy appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: If there’s one “trick” to achieving success regardless of skill, ability, or talent, it’s confidence . And the good news is it doesn’t necessarily have to be actual confidence. Merely the appearance of confidence is often enough to influence people and change outcomes. Confidence is how con men are able to rope people in, but confidence can also be used for good. If you learn how to exude confidence, it can be one of the most powerful tools for creating the life you want and effecting positive change in the world. So what does that look like, especially when you’re not really feeling it? We all wish we could walk boldly through the world without any worry or self-doubt, but most of us don’t feel 100% confident 100% of the time. That doesn’t mean we can’t appear confident, though. Former FBI agent and body language expert Joe Navarro shares six elements we need to understand in order to project confidence in a video for WIRED . 1. Understanding Confident Traits There are certain traits confident people have that help them appear comfortable when they walk into a room and command whatever space they are in. “When we talk about confidence, it’s so many things,” says Navarro. “It has to do with our posture, the way we present, how we look. Where’s our chin? Where are the eyes looking and gazing? Our gestures are loose, but they’re smoother. As we walk about, we walk as though we are on a mission.” Even how we move our eyeballs makes a difference. “The less confident we are, the less eye contact we make,” Navarro says. “The less confident we are, the more reluctant we are to look about.” People who are confident make more eye contact and look around more. Photo credit: Canva Confident people don’t show their confidence in the way many people assume. “I think sometimes people mistake machismo or theatrical displays of power as confidence,” Navarro adds. “Confidence can be very quiet.” The late Jane Goodall, for example, is not a loud-speaking person bursting with bravado. She’s rather meek and mild, and yet she commands every room. “One of the things you notice is they sort of have this command of themselves, and in doing so, that command transmits outward,” Navarro explains. You can also use time to convey confidence. Don’t rush, go at your own pace. “If you’re in charge, you’re in charge of time,” says Navarro. “I’m gonna take my time to walk out. I’m gonna take my time to answer your question. I will answer it in the pace, manner, and tone that I choose. And in doing that, we are demonstrating that we are confident and in control.” 2. Modeling Confidence One of the most effective ways of exuding confidence is to choose someone who is confident in a way that you admire and model yourself after them. What traits do they have that you could emulate? How do they move? How do they speak? How do people who are confident behave? Photo credit: Canva This doesn’t mean changing who you are on a fundamental level, but rather observing the people who have an ability you’re struggling with and behaving your way toward gaining that ability. “You know, we’re not born this way,” says Navarro. “These are things that we have to develop, and say, ‘How do I want to be perceived? And what can I do to achieve that?'” 3. Little Behaviors Navarro shares that little things can make a difference. For instance, indicating a direction by pointing with your finger is an undesirable behavior almost universally, but pointing with an open hand is not. Navarro shared an example from early in his law enforcement career, when he had to make an arrest. The first time he had to say, “Stop, you’re under arrest!” he said it in a high-pitched voice, and it sounded terrible. “You have to work at having that command presence, where you say [in a deeper voice], ‘Stop right there, don’t move.’ That’s almost theatrical, but it’s what is needed.” He gave another example of saying “No, stop,” with confidence, using a lower voice and an outstretched hand. The more confident you are in saying it, the more your fingers will spread apart. Those little behaviors convey confidence more than people realize. 4. Intonation We all have certain vocal habits that include how we use tone in our speaking. Navarro describes a phenomenon known as “uptalk,” which is when you raise your intonation at the end of phrases or sentences, almost as if you’re asking a question even when you’re not. He shared that speaking with confidence involves bringing your voice down in a more declarative way when you speak rather than sounding as if you’re questioning. Slowing down and using powerful pauses can make you appear confident. Photo credit: Canva 5. Cadence Many of us, especially when we’re not feeling comfortable or confident, talk too fast. But when you talk too fast, people stop listening. Pacing your speech and using pauses strategically can go a long way toward conveying confidence. “If you want people to listen to you, use cadence to get their attention, hold their attention, but then look forward to what that next set of words will be,” says Navarro. “It lets them know, at a subconscious level, this is the person in charge. And we know that they’re in charge because they have temporal control over this. They’re not in a hurry.” 6. Nonverbals People often think that confidence looks like holding your shoulders back, puffing up your chest, and keeping your chin up. It can look like that, says Navarro, but it doesn’t have to. Confidence can be conveyed in lots of nonverbal ways. Photo credit: Canva “You know, a lot of times confidence is just sitting comfortably in a chair. And that may have more to do with how much space you control. It may have to do with the gestures that you use.” When people look confident, their gestures are smooth. There’s no hesitation, quick movements, or jitteriness. They appear calm and in charge. When people are less confident, they feel like they have to hurry and answer right away. “Let’s face it: people are not born confident,” says Navarro. “They’re just not. We can become confident with the assistance of our parents who encourage us. We can become confident through our own achievements. We can become confident by going beyond our boundaries. But confidence is something that we can grow, we can nurture.” The bottom line on confidence Of course, we all want to feel truly confident and not just act like we are, but sometimes the behavior helps to create the feeling. “If you want to be confident, know your material, know the information, hone that skill, work at it, have that mastery of things, and of self,” says Navarro. “And that’s how you will come across as confident, no matter what your station in life is.” This article originally appeared in May. It has been updated. The post Body language expert reveals 6 keys to exuding confidence even if you’re not feeling it appeared first on Upworthy .

Today, he is raising their son, Kabir, alone. Purti never got to hold her baby, but her husband wants Kabir to know one thing: his mother fought until her last breath to meet him. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting Reading Time: 2 minutes PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting Understanding Beverage Container Evolution The beverage packaging industry continually seeks materials that balance structural integrity, consumer appeal, and environmental responsibility. Producers must evaluate various packaging formats to meet shifting regulatory demands and sustainability targets. Two prominent contenders in modern production lines are the traditional metal cylinder and the transparent polymer vessel. Understanding their distinct characteristics regarding material recovery and mass reduction helps brand owners make informed decisions for their product portfolios. The Mechanics of Lightweighting Lightweighting remains a primary strategy for reducing transport emissions and material consumption. Aluminium packaging has historically achieved significant mass reduction through advanced wall-ironing techniques, resulting in thin, rigid walls that withstand internal pressure. On the other hand, the PET can offers unique advantages in mass optimization because polymer distribution can be precisely controlled during the stretch blow molding process. This allows manufacturers to tailor wall thickness to specific product requirements, whether packaging still water or carbonated beverages. Recycling Infrastructure and Material Recovery End-of-life processing heavily influences the overall sustainability footprint of any packaging format. Metal recycling systems are globally mature, allowing aluminium to be melted down repeatedly without losing its core mechanical properties. Polymer recovery has also advanced significantly, with dedicated sorting facilities capable of processing clear and colored containers efficiently. Both materials fit into circular economy models, though the specific infrastructure varies by geographic region. Key Production Considerations When selecting between these two packaging formats, producers must analyze several operational factors: Filling line compatibility and conversion costs for existing equipment Barrier properties required to protect product shelf life against oxygen and light Consumer perception of touch, transparency, and tactile experience Supply chain resilience and raw material price volatility Balancing Sustainability Goals Ultimately, the choice between metal and polymer containers depends on specific brand priorities and distribution models. While metal provides permanent recyclability, polymers offer design versatility and complete product visibility. By carefully assessing lightweighting potential and local recovery streams, producers can optimize their packaging strategy for long-term operational success. items.descriptionOriginal: Take a walk through a city park. There are trees lining the paths, lawns stretching between them and plenty of shade. It looks green, perhaps even thriving. But where are the wild grasses that feed grazing animals? The flowering shrubs that attract butterflies? The ponds and stream banks where birds and other creatures find food and shelter? A place can look green while losing what wildlife needs to survive. That is the message emerging from Chandigarh's 2026 wildlife survey. Researchers recorded an impressive range of species, from a leopard and sambar deer to birds and butterflies. Yet they also found that several native trees were struggling to regenerate naturally and recommended greater protection for grasslands, wetlands and other habitats. For Indian cities, where planting drives often signal environmental progress, the findings suggest a better starting point: the habitat and the life it supports. What the survey found in Chandigarh's forests Conducted between 20 and 27 November 2025 by the Chandigarh Department of Forest and Wildlife and the Wildlife Institute of India (WII), the assessment covered Sukhna Wildlife Sanctuary and forest patches beyond its boundaries. Researchers documented 16 mammal species, 132 bird species, 73 butterfly species and 13 species of reptiles and amphibians. They also recorded 43 tree species, 14 shrub species and 22 herb species. The survey detected a leopard and estimated around 603 sambar, a deer species found in the region's forests. The figures show the variety of life these natural areas continue to shelter. But counting species was only one part of the exercise. The report also looked at the condition of their habitats and recommended restoring native vegetation, protecting grasslands, reviving wetlands and streamside habitats, and controlling invasive species. In Chandigarh, the survey recorded 49 butterfly species in riparian habitats, the areas alongside streams, rivers and other waterbodies. Photograph: (The Tribune) Knowing which animals live in a forest matters. Knowing whether their habitat can continue to support them tells us what needs attention. A forest can have trees and still need help Imagine a woodland full of mature trees. From a distance, it might seem healthy. Look beneath the canopy, though, and there may be very few young trees coming up to replace the older ones. This is the problem of poor natural regeneration, which the Chandigarh survey flagged in native species including khair ( Senegalia catechu ), siris ( Albizia lebbeck ), Lannea coromandelica and Terminalia anogeissiana . Natural regeneration is simply the process of seeds becoming new plants without people planting them. It allows a forest to renew itself across generations. If young trees are missing, some native species could become less common as older trees die. That is why an increase in tree cover cannot, by itself, tell us whether a forest is doing well. The survey also cautioned against large plantations dominated by one species, known as monocultures. A row of identical trees may offer shade, but a healthy habitat needs different kinds of vegetation, from tall trees to shrubs, grasses and ground cover. Each layer has a purpose. Birds need places to nest, butterflies seek nectar, insects live among leaves and grasses, and herbivores depend on suitable plants for food. The report recommends replacing invasive vegetation with native species. Why does that matter? Why native plants can make a difference Native plants occur naturally in a region. Over time, they develop relationships with the insects, birds and animals around them. Some insects feed on particular plants; birds visit their flowers; other animals carry their seeds to new places. Introduced, or exotic, plants come from elsewhere. Many grow successfully in cities, and some offer flowers, fruit or shelter. But they do not always support the same relationships. Certain species can also spread so aggressively that they push out local vegetation. A 2023 Bengaluru study published in Science of the Total Environment helps explain why the distinction matters. Researchers compared how birds and mammals interacted with native and alien trees. They found that taller native trees with larger floral displays supported more bird species than alien trees with comparable displays. There was another interesting difference. Nectar-feeding birds were more likely to visit native flowers in ways that helped pollination. On alien trees, their visits more often involved 'nectar theft', where a bird takes nectar without transferring pollen in the way the flower needs to reproduce. This does not mean every introduced tree is harmful. The study recognised that alien trees can provide resources for wildlife in cities where natural vegetation has already been lost. The lesson is to understand what different plants actually offer local wildlife, rather than choosing them only because they grow quickly or look attractive. For Chandigarh, that supports the survey's recommendation to prioritise native vegetation that belongs to the landscape. Why an open grassland deserves protection A patch of tall, wild grass might look like an empty plot beside a landscaped park. It is easy to imagine someone deciding to plant trees there to 'improve' it. But a grassland is already a habitat. Its native grasses feed grazing animals, shelter insects and support species that depend on open spaces. Their roots also help hold soil together and influence how rainwater moves through the ground. Planting trees across an existing grassland can change the conditions that make it useful to those species. The result may look greener to us while offering less to the wildlife that lived there. For cities designing parks, the type of vegetation and its surroundings can matter as much as tree numbers. Photograph: (Chandigarh Help Post) This is why the Chandigarh survey specifically recommended protecting grasslands and restoring native grasses, including Eulaliopsis binata , Arundinella nepalensis and Heteropogon contortus . Across India, open spaces are often treated as land waiting to be developed, tidied up or planted over. Planners first need to ask what habitat is already there. Sometimes, caring for a green space means leaving room for its grasses to grow. Wetlands and riverbanks support different kinds of life The same principle applies to waterbodies and the land around them. In Chandigarh, the survey recorded 49 butterfly species in riparian habitats, the areas alongside streams, rivers and other waterbodies. Woodland habitats, meanwhile, recorded the highest bird diversity. These differences matter. A forest, an open grassland and a stream bank may all be part of the same landscape, yet each offers food and shelter to different species. The report therefore called for wetland restoration and better care of streamside habitats , alongside other measures such as controlling invasive species. Research from the East Kolkata Wetlands shows why protecting such spaces requires attention to more than their size or appearance. A 2024 study in Environmental Research examined changes between 1991 and 2023. It found that the number of wetland patches had risen from 2,689 to 4,532, a sign that the landscape had become more fragmented. Over the same period, the study's ecosystem health index fell from 0.67 to 0.55. In simple terms, a wetland can still appear on a city map while its connected habitats are broken into smaller pieces and its ecological condition deteriorates. The Kolkata findings do not describe Chandigarh's wetlands, but they show what cities risk overlooking if they focus only on how much green or blue space remains. The two-day Capacity Building Workshop on Wildlife Survey & Techniques concluded today in Chandigarh! Diverse participants— representatives of civil society organisations, college students, wildlife enthusiasts, media personnel and journalists were sensitized and trained on various wildlife survey and monitoring methods. Thank all the multiple stakeholders for making it impactful. #WildlifeConservation #CitizenScience #WildlifeSurvey #Chandigarh #Sukhna #Chandigarhbirdclub @moefcc @wii_india @GobindsagarBha1 @RuchiBadola2 @gopigv @UDHAYAR230 @Ashik40405287 @Alexjacob11 @NonitaRana04 @RayR5847 — Wildlife Institute of India (@wii_india) November 19, 2025 Chandigarh's survey also recorded the red-eared slider turtle, an exotic aquatic species, and recommended its removal and management in controlled settings. Such species are sometimes released into waterbodies after being kept as pets and can place additional pressure on native wildlife. Wetlands need care as living habitats, not simply as water-filled spaces. What should other Indian cities measure? There is evidence from Delhi, too, that a park's value to wildlife depends on more than its tree count. A 2024 study in Ecological Frontiers examined birds across 64 city parks, recording 90 species and 19,131 individual birds. It found that vegetation characteristics and disturbance affected which birds used the parks. Native trees and lower surrounding urbanisation were also linked with greater bird diversity. For cities designing parks, the type of vegetation and its surroundings can matter as much as tree numbers. Chandigarh's plantation figures offer another lesson. During 2025–26, the administration planted 6,64,133 saplings against a target of 5,76,221. But third-party monitoring in November 2025 and March 2026 found an overall survival rate of around 79%. For 2026–27, the administration lowered its target to 4,19,854 saplings, including those distributed and sold, and said it would pay greater attention to site selection, quality and care after planting. Survival is important. So is asking whether the right species have been planted in the right place, and whether existing habitats are being protected rather than replaced. The Chandigarh survey was conducted over a short period, so its findings are a snapshot rather than proof that the city's wildlife populations are rising or falling. Longer-term, seasonal monitoring would help show how these habitats and their inhabitants change. But its message is already useful. Before the next plantation drive, city planners can ask a few practical questions: Is this land a forest, grassland or wetland? Which species rely on it? Are young native plants growing back? And what does this place need most? For some spaces, the answer will be trees. For others, it may be restoring a stream bank, protecting a grassland or allowing native shrubs to return. A city's natural wealth lives in more than its canopy. It is in the butterflies visiting riverbanks, the birds sheltering in woodland, the deer grazing on native grasses and the many smaller creatures that depend on them. Making room for all these habitats is how a city makes room for wildlife. Sources: 'Restore native species, wetlands; curb invasives: UT wildlife survey' : By Munieshwer A, Published on 2 October 2026 'Chandigarh's Wildlife Survey Exposes the Cost of Neglecting Native Habitats' : By Urban Acres, Published on 2 October 2026 'Urban park characteristics defining avian community structure in Delhi, India' : By Deepti Kumari, Ashutosh Srivastava, Upamanyu Hore, Published in December 2024 'Native fauna interact differently with native and alien trees in a tropical megacit' : By Purabi Deshpande, Rohan Sharma, Aleksi Lehikoinen, Rose Thorogood, Published on 10 April 2023 'Wildlife Week 2026 inaugurated in Chandigarh with Walkathon; focus on habitat connectivity and wildlife conservation' : By India News Calling, Published on 2 October 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: When people coined the proverb that “mighty oaks from little acorns grow”, they certainly weren’t thinking of Lyme disease. But literal acorns—not poetic metaphors—turn out to play a surprisingly big role in the spread of this mighty tick-borne illness, according to a recent paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . A surge in acorns one year can translate into a boom two years later in the population of ticks that transmit the disease to people. This discovery illustrates the ways in which a web of tiny, interconnected things—acorns, mice, microbes—can have big and unexpected consequences for people. It also shows that it can take decades of scientific research to decipher the head-scratching complexity of ecosystems. The results are “helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said Shannon LaDeau, one of the paper’s authors and an ecologist with the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York State’s Hudson River Valley. LaDeau and colleague Richard Ostfeld oversee a Lyme-related research program at the institute that stretches back more than 30 years, just a few decades after the disease was first identified. Over that time, scientists have turned plots of New York forestland into an outdoor Lyme laboratory. They’ve assembled mountains of data tracking the ups and downs of a huge range of elements: temperature, rainfall, oak seedlings, mouse populations, tick numbers, infection rates, you name it. The results have repeatedly surprised scientists, defying expectations about the disease. It’s been known since the 1980s that the disease is caused by the bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi. The bite of an infected deer tick transmits the bacterium to people, causing flu-like symptoms that can escalate to chronic fatigue, memory loss, depression and even brain swelling and cardiac problems. More than 450,000 cases are reported in the U.S. each year, plus more than 200,000 in Europe. Despite the tick’s association with deer, the Cary Institute work didn’t bear out initial suspicions that more white-tailed deer translated into more dangers for people. The researchers found no correlation between deer numbers and the abundance of tick nymphs—the life stage when they most commonly transmit the disease to people. Lyme Disease: Prescribed fire Instead, the researchers uncovered evidence of a cascade of cause and effect between oak trees, white-footed mice and ticks. Acorns from red oak trees at the study sites are a primary food source for the mice. The year after a big acorn harvest, the mouse population boomed, the scientists found. The mice, in turn, are a prime feeding target for larval ticks which go on to become nymphs the following year. A big year for mice translated into a roughly 40% increase in abundance of tick nymphs the next year. All this thanks to a bumper crop in acorns two years earlier. While acorns aren’t abundant everywhere that the disease occurs, fluctuations in other crucial mouse food, such as seeds, could have the same effect, the scientists wrote. While it took years to tease apart these dynamics, researchers were still puzzled by other patterns. A surge in mice meant more ticks—and therefore a greater risk of people getting infected. But it didn’t translate into a higher percentage of the ticks themselves carrying the disease, the data showed. “It kept me up at night,” Ostfeld said of the result. “It meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.” An apparent answer emerged when the researchers looked not just at the mouse population, but at a variety of small mammals. The long-term study plots were located in relatively intact forest that supported a range of other warm-blooded critters, such as skunks, squirrels and opossums. Many of these creatures are less prone to getting infected when a tick feeds on them, which also means they are less likely to spread the bacteria to other ticks. As a consequence, the percentage of infected ticks was driven not just by the number of mice but the population of a range of creatures. By contrast, in nearby places where forests had been broken into pieces by human intrusion , the diversity of small mammals was smaller. In those spots, where ticks had fewer options, higher mouse numbers did translate into more infected ticks. So in addition to small things like acorns, add two very big things that shape people’s risk of encountering Lyme disease: loss of habitat and of biodiversity. items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, once the paddy harvest is over, farmers across Haryana face a familiar problem. Their fields are covered with leftover straw, and they need to clear the land before planting the next crop. For many, burning this stubble is the quickest solution. But the smoke that rises from these fields adds to North India's already severe air pollution. Now imagine if that same straw could earn money, create jobs and even help power industries. That's exactly what two women from Haryana and neighbouring Rajasthan set out to do. Sanjana, a graduate from Ghoranwali village in Haryana's Sirsa district, and her friend Sonika, from Bhadra in Rajasthan, saw a business opportunity in something farmers struggled to get rid of. They decided to collect leftover paddy straw , locally called parali , and turn it into biofuel pellets that power plants could use as an alternative fuel. In 2024, they started SSAR Biomass Green Private Limited with an investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore. Today, the venture reports an annual turnover of Rs 7–8 crore and employs over 20 people. From a pollution problem to a business idea For Sonika, the idea began with a sight she had witnessed repeatedly after the paddy harvest: thick smoke spreading across the sky as farmers burned crop residue. Concerned about the environmental and public health consequences, she began thinking about how this agricultural waste could be put to better use. Rather than treating stubble burning as a problem with no easy solution, she and Sanjana started exploring ways to convert the residue into a commercially useful product. At their manufacturing unit in Ghoranwali, Haryana, machinery processes leftover paddy straw into compact biofuel pellets, giving agricultural waste a productive use. Photograph: ( Peddler media ) The idea was to address two needs together: give farmers a productive use for their leftover crop residue while creating an alternative fuel that industries could use. Government policies and initiatives promoting stubble management also helped create an opportunity for the venture to take shape. Building a factory around farm waste In 2024, Sanjana and Sonika set up their manufacturing unit in Ghoranwali with an investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) scheme. The factory follows a process that begins in the fields. The women source paddy straw through baler operators in Sirsa and surrounding areas. These operators collect and compress the loose residue, making it easier to transport and store. The stubble is then brought to their factory, where machinery processes it into compact biofuel pellets. These pellets can be supplied to power plants as an alternative fuel. By sourcing paddy straw from farmers and baler operators across the region, the founders are creating a market for crop residue. Photograph: (AI generated using reference) The scale of the operation is considerable. The unit uses approximately 1 lakh to 1.5 lakh quintals of paddy stubble every year. Since the raw material is available mainly during the harvesting season, the founders also have to plan for the months ahead. They collect and store the residue after harvest, ensuring that the factory has enough raw material to continue production throughout the year. This seasonal sourcing and year-round production model allows them to keep the business running beyond the harvesting window. From discarded straw to a growing rural enterprise The venture's impact extends beyond the pellets it produces. By creating a market for paddy straw, SSAR Biomass Green Private Limited also generates business opportunities for local baler operators and others involved in collecting and transporting the residue. The factory itself provides employment to more than 20 people, bringing work opportunities closer to home for residents in and around the village. From an initial investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore, Sanjana and Sonika have built an enterprise reporting an annual turnover of Rs 7–8 crore. What began as an effort to address stubble burning has grown into a rural enterprise that employs over 20 people and reports an annual turnover of Rs 8 crore. Photograph: ( Peddler Media ) For the two founders, the next harvest season will bring another opportunity to source more stubble, keep production going and expand their business. Their work has given farmers in the region another possible route for managing crop residue, while creating a market for material that would otherwise have little economic value. In Ghoranwali, the paddy harvest no longer marks just the end of a farming cycle. For Sanjana and Sonika, it also marks the beginning of another season of business, one built around putting farm waste to productive use. Sources: '2 women turn paddy stubble into Rs 8-crore business in Haryana' by Anil Kakkar for The Tribune, Published on 14 October 2026. items.descriptionOriginal: A road outside a forest stays lit after sunset. So does a nearby place of worship or a cluster of shops where people gather. Those lights help people go about their lives. But their glow can travel beyond the places they are meant to illuminate. For wildlife living in Kerala's Western Ghats, that raises an important question: how much of the night inside protected forests is still naturally dark? A team of four researchers has begun answering it. Their study, published in Biological Conservation in October 2026, mapped artificial light in and around 21 protected areas in Kerala and examined the roads, buildings and other human activities associated with it. Their findings reveal a conservation concern that is easy to overlook: even where forests have protected boundaries, light from surrounding areas can still reach them. What's causing the forests to light up? Using satellite data from 2024, researchers S. Haripriya, M.S. Arjun, S. Gopakumar and Vijayan Divya measured night-time light across national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. They then compared those measurements with maps showing nearby roads, places of worship, buildings and centres of human activity. The difference between forests was striking. Periyar Tiger Reserve's western division recorded the highest average and peak levels of satellite-measured light among the 21 areas, with a mean radiance of 0.369 and a maximum of 24.0. Kerala's protected areas include tropical evergreen forests, semi-evergreen forests, shola-grassland ecosystems and riverine habitats. Photograph: (Tiger Safari Tours India) Within protected areas, the strongest statistical link was with the density of places of worship. In the surrounding landscape, road networks and places where people gather or work were more important predictors. That distinction matters. Light affecting a forest may be associated with several kinds of human activity, and managing it requires knowing where to look. But light does not always arrive as a visible beam. It can scatter through the atmosphere and brighten the night sky over places some distance away. Researchers call this skyglow . The team examined areas extending up to 30 km beyond forest boundaries. Their modelling suggested that the wider surrounding landscape, particularly the 10–30 km zone, could contribute substantially to skyglow. This means lighting decisions made several kilometres away may influence how dark a protected forest remains at night. Why does darkness matter to wildlife? The Western Ghats are home to many species found nowhere else, including animals active after dark. Natural cycles of light and darkness help wildlife navigate, find food and follow daily rhythms. Research elsewhere has shown that artificial lighting can alter animal behaviour. However, the Kerala study did not directly observe animals or measure how they were affected. That distinction is important. The researchers have identified where artificial light is present and which features of the surrounding landscape are associated with it. Understanding what those light levels mean for different species will require further research. Lead author S. Haripriya has also expressed an interest in investigating these ecological effects in future. Could simple lighting changes help protect these forests? For forest departments and local authorities, the study offers something immediately useful: a way to identify areas where lighting deserves closer attention. A brightly lit road near a forest edge could be assessed for lamps that shine upwards or sideways. Places of worship and tourism facilities could review whether lights need to remain on at full strength throughout the night. Shielded fixtures, lower-intensity lighting and switching off unnecessary lights during periods of low activity are among the options worth considering, while keeping public safety in mind. Periyar Tiger Reserve's western division recorded the highest average and peak levels of satellite-measured light among the 21 areas, with a mean radiance of 0.369 and a maximum of 24.0. Photograph: (Deccan Herald) These are possible next steps rather than changes already implemented because of the study. The findings could, however, help forest officials, local communities and those responsible for public lighting decide where action would be most useful. For years, protecting forests has meant paying attention to what happens within their boundaries. This research offers a reason to look beyond those boundaries, too. And sometimes, protecting a forest's natural environment may begin with something as simple as reconsidering where, when and how we use light. Sources: 'Spatial assessment of artificial light at night in and around protected areas of the Kerala Western Ghats' : By S. Haripriya, M.S. Arjun, S. Gopakumar and Vijayan Divya 'From illumination expansion to ecological response: artificial light at night and detectability of forest vegetation responses across India' : By Dibyendu Dutta, Published on 31 October 2026 'New study examines effect of artificial light at night in protected areas' : By Arathi Menon, Published on 5 November 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: A patch of dust near a busy road, smoke rising from an industrial chimney, and waste burning in an open space may all contribute to a city's air pollution. But the sources responsible for poor air quality are not necessarily the same across neighbourhoods. This means that a measure addressing pollution in one part of a city may not be equally effective elsewhere. Understanding what contributes to poor air quality at specific locations is therefore an important part of planning cleaner cities . Ahmedabad is attempting to address this challenge by looking beyond citywide air-quality readings and examining pollution at specific locations. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, has identified 10 locations across the city for a real-time air-quality monitoring initiative called SMART-VAYU. Reported by The Times of India (TOI) on September 30, 2026, the project aims to identify local pollution hotspots, trace the sources of emissions and generate data that can help civic authorities plan targeted interventions. Initial monitoring exercises at two locations — Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex and Narendra Modi Stadium — have already revealed how pollution sources can differ within the same city. One city, two different pollution profiles The initial findings from Ahmedabad offer an interesting look at how the sources contributing to air pollution can vary from one location to another. In its October 17, 2026 report, TOI detailed the findings from air-quality sampling at the Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex and Narendra Modi Stadium. Sampling at the riverfront was conducted between May 4 and May 24, while monitoring at Narendra Modi Stadium took place between June 25 and August 8. At the Sabarmati Riverfront, dust accounted for 36% of the estimated source contribution, compared with 23% at Narendra Modi Stadium. Coal combustion contributed 24% at the riverfront, while its estimated contribution at the stadium was just 1%. The pattern was different at Motera. The combined category of marine emissions and refuse burning accounted for 38% of the estimated pollution sources at Narendra Modi Stadium, compared with 16% at the riverfront. Power plant-related sources contributed another 20% at the stadium. The analysis also examined different types of organic aerosols. Traffic-related organic aerosols contributed 18% at Narendra Modi Stadium and 13% at the riverfront. Solid-fuel combustion-related organic aerosols accounted for 16% at the stadium and 5% at the riverfront. These findings highlight an important aspect of urban air pollution: even within one city, different locations can have different pollution profiles . Understanding these differences can help authorities identify which sources need attention in specific areas, rather than approaching air pollution as a uniform problem across the city. Why Ahmedabad is looking beyond citywide AQI readings Identifying the sources behind air pollution is not always straightforward. Citywide air-quality readings provide information about pollution levels, but understanding what is contributing to poor air quality in a particular neighbourhood requires more detailed monitoring. This is the gap that SMART-VAYU aims to address. The initiative stands for Sensing and Monitoring for Air Quality using Real-time Technology – Vision-based Ahmedabad air analysis for Urban Management. The project involves three broad components: mapping existing pollution sources, establishing a hyperlocal monitoring network and developing a decision-support system for urban air-quality management. For civic authorities, this distinction could help connect monitoring with specific pollution-control measures. Photograph: (Ahmedabad Mirror) For this, AMC and IIT Kanpur finalised 10 monitoring locations across Ahmedabad. These include Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex, Narendra Modi Stadium, Gujarat Police Academy at Karai, Sanskardham, Veer Savarkar Sports Complex, Pirana AMC community service centre, Rakhial AMC health office, Vatva GIDC's Chandrakala complex, Bopal urban health centre and Thaltej AMC ward office. The selection considered meteorological conditions, particulate matter readings, annual wind patterns, satellite-based aerosol optical depth and estimated PM2.5 concentrations. Practical requirements such as electricity, security, accessibility and airflow were also taken into account. The plan is to deploy five locations with mobile laboratory sampling alongside sensors, while the remaining five will have fixed sensors. The wider project envisages eventually expanding the network to around 400 sensors across Ahmedabad. How the monitoring network will identify pollution sources Unlike conventional monitoring systems that primarily provide broader air-quality readings, these sensors will continuously measure pollutants such as PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide. They will also record meteorological parameters, including temperature and humidity. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, has identified 10 locations across the city for a real-time air-quality monitoring. Photograph: (Hindustan Times) An important component is the mobile Real-Time Source Apportionment Laboratory (RTSA), which will help examine the contribution of different pollution sources. Source apportionment is the process of estimating how much different sources contribute to the pollutants present in the air. These could include vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road dust, construction and waste burning. By examining these contributions, the initiative aims to generate pollution hotspot maps, forecasts and alerts that can help authorities identify locations requiring attention. From identifying pollution to planning targeted action Ahmedabad already has an air-quality monitoring network under the Centre's System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting and Research (SAFAR) programme. Its monitoring stations provide city-level air-quality information and forecasts. SMART-VAYU seeks to add another layer of information by examining pollution sources at specific locations. For civic authorities, this distinction could help connect monitoring with specific pollution-control measures. For instance, identifying road dust as a major contributor could inform dust-control and road-cleaning measures. Similarly, evidence of industrial emissions or waste burning could help direct inspections and enforcement. The effectiveness of the initiative will depend on how consistently the monitoring network operates, whether its findings translate into enforceable measures and how improvements in air quality are tracked over time. Ultimately, Ahmedabad's initiative highlights why tackling urban air pollution requires more than understanding how polluted a city is. It also requires knowing what is polluting different parts of it. Because when pollution sources vary from one neighbourhood to another, the solutions must account for those differences too. Sources: 'Ahmedabad: SMART-VAYU to zoom in on air pollution hotspots' : By Kapil Dave, Published on 30 September 2026 'Ahmedabad maps pollution hotspots ahead of 2030 Commonwealth Games' : By Meghdoot Sharon, Published on 17 October 2026 'IIT-K Ahmedabad Gets Real-Time Pollution Tracking Activity' : By Kotak School of Sustainability - IIT Kanpur

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Students Giving Tennis a Second Serve Reading Time: 4 minutes A student-run nonprofit born in Flower Mound, Texas, now keeps used tennis balls out of landfills in 16 states. A single tennis ball weighs about two ounces. That is easy to overlook, because nobody throws away just one. Since 2024, BallBack , a student-led nonprofit based in Flower Mound, Texas, has recycled or repurposed more than 160,000 of them. At roughly 58 grams apiece, that is about 9.3 metric tons of rubber and felt, a little over 20,000 pounds. Every one of those balls was headed for the trash. According to RecycleBalls, a tennis ball takes roughly 400 years to break down, slowly shedding microplastics into the surrounding soil. Curbside recycling programs do not accept them. The national picture is larger still. The United States discards an estimated 125 million tennis balls each year, or about 340,000 a day. By comparison, 160,000 balls is less than half a day of the country’s tennis ball waste. What makes BallBack interesting is not only its total so far, but how quickly a model built by high school students is spreading, and how easily it can be copied by anyone with a court, a school, and a car. BallBack began with Prem Kamasani, a varsity tennis player at Flower Mound High School. After practice one evening, he watched his coach getting ready to throw out roughly 400 used balls. He asked whether he could take them instead. “I noticed hundreds of balls going to the trash every week, and no one was doing anything about it,” Kamasani says on BallBack’s website. The balls went home with him. Some went to animal shelters as toys, and others ended up under school chairs. He then began calling local tennis centers to ask whether they had balls to give away as well. Most did. The collection outgrew his family’s garage, then several garages, and teammates joined in. A Lead4Change grant helped turn the school project into a national organization, spreading to over 310 members in 2026. The funding covered prepaid shipping, so courts anywhere in the country could send in their balls at no cost. Partnerships spread across Dallas–Fort Worth, from public facilities such as Kiest and Samuell Grand tennis centers to SMU’s college tennis program and the Flower Mound Animal Shelter. BallBack’s process is deliberately simple. A chapter leader places a free, branded collection bin at a partner facility, such as a tennis center, club, school, or homeowners’ association. Players drop off dead balls after practice instead of tossing them in the trash. Nobody on site has to sort or clean anything. Leaders monitor fill levels and stop by once or twice a month before anything overflows. Recycling bins at Samuell Grand Tennis Center in Dallas, one of BallBack’s partner facilities, let players drop off used tennis balls instead of throwing them away. Photo courtesy of BallBack . Sorting comes next, and it reflects the organization’s priorities. Balls that still bounce are never shredded. They go back into play through youth tennis programs and school teams that cannot afford new equipment, as well as other repurposing partners. Others go to dog shelters as enrichment toys, or to senior living communities, where they serve as walker feet. BallBack boxes only the balls with no play left in them, labels them with prepaid UPS shipping, and sends them to RecycleBalls or the USTA, BallBack’s national recycling partners. There, they separate the rubber and felt and grind them into crumb rubber that becomes new tennis court surfaces, playground padding, and footing for equestrian arenas. Through RecycleBalls and USTA, BallBack’s shipments help feed a North American collection network of roughly 10,000 locations. BallBack now runs with a national team of students recruited from across the country, each responsible for a distinct part of the work. The media team shapes how BallBack tells its story, from pickup-day footage to chapter spotlights. The marketing team carries that story to new schools, players, and facilities. The onboarding team brings each new chapter leader up to speed with step-by-step guides, so a student in Seattle or Fort Lauderdale can complete a first pickup within a week of signing up. Leaders trade questions and progress in a shared online community. This structure lets the network grow without relying on any one person. BallBack now counts 31 student chapter leaders across 16 states, more than 310 members, and over 55 partner facilities. Chapters operate in New York City, Philadelphia, Chicago, Portland, Seattle, Minneapolis, Folsom, and Green Bay, among other cities. In Manhattan, one senior ships roughly 750 balls a month. In Falls Church, Virginia, chapter leader Surya Arivumani has already recycled more than 1,200. BallBack is set up so that taking part does not depend on where you live. High school sophomores, juniors, and rising seniors in any U.S. city without an existing chapter can apply to start one at their local school. The commitment is one or two pickup trips a month, an hour or two each, for at least four months. Costs are close to zero, and leaders unlock $60 in credit after their first shipment. New chapter leaders are accepted every quarter. Tennis facilities near an existing chapter can list themselves as operating partners and receive free bins, pickups, and shipping. Facilities elsewhere can join as affiliate partners and ship their own boxes for free using prepaid FedEx labels. Individuals with a bag of old balls in the garage can also request a free shipping label, pack a box, and drop it off at FedEx. In Dallas–Fort Worth, anyone with 100 or more balls can arrange a free pickup. BallBack’s next milestone is a world record for the most tennis balls recycled in a single week. The plan is a coordinated national recycling week in spring of 2027. Chapter leaders, members, and partner facilities nationwide would collect, sort, and ship tennis balls at the same time. The effort is still being organized, as BallBack has yet to choose an adjudicator to set the rules for counting and verifying the balls. Whatever the final tally, the week is designed to do what no single chapter can: show what happens when hundreds of courts in dozens of cities choose to recycle at once. Long before BallBack, Kamasani’s father sent him to gather old balls from behind their neighborhood courts instead of buying new ones. Today, Kamasani mentors student leaders he’s never met in cities he’s never visited, who are doing the same thing on a national scale. In BallBack’s latest milestone update, he wrote that the 160,000 mark showed what “a bin by the fence and a student with a car” can accomplish. Students interested in starting a chapter, facilities that want to host a bin, and players with balls to donate can find details at ballback.org . The post The Students Giving Tennis a Second Serve appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Japanese Scientists Design a Plant-Based Plastic that can Become Fertilizer Reading Time: 3 minutes Researchers at Chiba University have developed a flexible, plant-based plastic that can be turned into crop fertilizer after use. Plant-based plastic often ends up in the same places as ordinary plastic, from landfills to incinerators. A research team in Japan wants to give it a more useful ending. What if a used plastic film could help grow the next crop? Associate Professor Daisuke Aoki of Chiba University led the study . Colleagues from the University of Tokyo and Tohoku University joined the work. They published their results in the journal Scientific Reports in August 2026. The need for new ideas is growing. Global plastic use reached 460 million metric tons in 2019, according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. If current trends continue, it could climb to 1.2 billion metric tons by 2060. Recycling and waste-to-energy plants are struggling to keep pace with this growth. Aoki’s team took a different route by designing a plastic with its end-of-life already planned. The material starts with isosorbide, a nontoxic compound made from glucose. Glucose is a simple sugar that can come from plant starch, such as corn. Chemists link isosorbide units into a clear, hard plastic called poly(isosorbide carbonate). In 2021, Aoki and his students showed that warm ammonia water breaks down this plastic. The process splits it back into isosorbide and urea. Urea is one of the world’s most widely used nitrogen fertilizers. Aoki compared the goal to the Haber-Bosch process, which turned nitrogen from the air into fertilizer a century ago. His team hoped to turn plastic waste into food in a similar way. Their conversion also needed no costly metal catalysts. One problem remained. The original plastic was hard and brittle, stretching only about 4% before it snapped. That limited it to a narrow range of rigid products. Most plastics are softened with additives called plasticizers. Common ones, such as phthalates, do not break down into anything useful. Some also raise health concerns. The Chiba team designed a plasticizer for its plant-based plastic from the same building block. It has an isosorbide core linked to two short triethylene glycol chains, a common industrial chemical. Like the plastic, it breaks apart when treated with ammonia. With the new plasticizer, the material stretched about 45% before breaking, more than ten times as far as before. It also began to soften at about 40 degrees Celsius instead of 161 degrees, a sign of greater flexibility. Unlike a phthalate blend, the new mix stayed clear and uniform at every mixing ratio. The phthalate version turned cloudy, indicating its ingredients had separated. The team also made a longer-chain version of the plasticizer that stretched the plastic even further. It could be made at yields above 80%, versus under 25% for the first version. That makes it more practical to produce at scale. Converting the used plastic is simple. The team heated it in ammonia water at 90 degrees Celsius for 24 hours. The solid plastic dissolved completely into a clear liquid. That liquid held most of the original building blocks. The team recovered about 98% of the isosorbide, 78% of the possible urea, and 90% of the glycol. Some carbon escaped as carbon dioxide, and better conditions could raise the urea yield. Next came the most important test. The researchers used the liquid as fertilizer without any purification. They tried it on a common lab plant and on komatsuna, a leafy green often called Japanese mustard spinach. Over 36 days in a greenhouse, komatsuna grown with the recycled product matched plants fed commercial urea. Both groups grew far better than plants given no nitrogen. In the lab, the product performed at least as well as urea alone. Komatsuna grown with fertilizer from recycled plant-based plastic matched plants fed commercial urea. Photo courtesy of Scientific Reports . The authors are clear about the limits. Their plant-based plastic is not biodegradable, so it only becomes fertilizer after chemical treatment. Its strength is also not yet high enough for demanding uses. Other questions remain open. The team has not yet tested whether the plasticizer leaks out over time. They also have not measured the full energy cost and environmental footprint of the conversion process. Even so, the researchers see clear uses ahead. This plant-based plastic could be used for agricultural mulch films, seedling pots, shopping bags, and packaging. Farms could then turn used films and pots into fertilizer on site. Aoki believes plastics are at a turning point. He hopes people will one day see plastic waste as a valuable resource for growing food rather than trash. If that happens, plant-based plastic could complete a full circle. Plant-based material would return to the soil to feed new plants. The post Japanese Scientists Design a Plant-Based Plastic that can Become Fertilizer appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: “Just eat less.” “Work harder.” “Have some willpower.” We hear it all the time. But if weight loss were that simple, why can keeping it off feel even harder? Because sometimes, your own biology pushes back. After you lose weight, your body can respond with stronger hunger signals and lower energy use. These biological adaptations can favour weight regain. Does that mean weight always comes back? No. It means long-term medical support may need more than a short burst of willpower. And struggling doesn’t mean someone is lazy or lacks discipline. Weight is shaped by biology, behaviour and environment. If you keep struggling, continue with practical nutrition, movement, strength and sleep habits. And if weight repeatedly returns, or the plan feels impossible to sustain, speak to a qualified doctor about long-term weight management and the biological or practical barriers involved. Getting medical support is not failure. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight management. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #WeightRegain #WeightManagement #Biology #HealthJourney [why weight comes back after weight loss, body pushes back after weight loss, hunger signals and weight regain, struggling with weight is not a character flaw, India]

items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Get smart Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans. Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. Will says: As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. Mapping roots In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. “I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.” Becca says: On the one hand, using an app takes away the serendipity of just happening into a notable tree. On the other hand, I do like the idea of people detouring to see cool trees . What else we’re reading Minnesota announces ‘effective end’ to veteran homelessness, achieving decades-long goal — shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas from KSTP Free tool helps young men to take responsibility for sexual harm — shared by Contributing Editor Geetanjali Krishna from Positive News ‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis? — shared by Michaela Haas from the Guardian In other news… Turns out people love moss! Our Instagram video about how moss is taking over cities has really taken off. To learn more about all the cool things moss can do, read Michaela Haas’s great story. The post What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: At fourteen, Shakhzoda Saidova slipped away from a conference table with the UN General Assembly and UNICEF in Tajikistan — too nervous, too convinced she didn't belong. What brought her back was a single sentence from a mentor: stay true to what you're actually hearing from inside. That line has followed her into every room since. She grew up in a country where her mother — who finished school with perfect marks and won a law scholarship — was forbidden by her husband's family from ever practicing as a lawyer. Watching that buried ambition became Shakhzoda's compass. Now studying in Romania, she is building SafeVoice: a disarmingly simple website listing real lawyers and crisis shelter numbers for women in Tajikistan facing domestic violence, because she knows what it costs a woman with three children and one free minute to find a page of dead links. She speaks five languages and is already being criticized for living in Europe at nineteen instead of being married. What's striking is the image of her mother, smiling serenely at those who disapprove — "Yes, I allowed that; yes, she's my daughter" — after accepting her daughter's diploma while the teenager boarded a flight towards a future she herself was never allowed to choose.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Mycelium Leather at Mass-Production Scale Moves Closer to Reality Reading Time: 3 minutes Finnish researchers found a way to make mycelium leather at mass-production scale using papermaking methods. Mycelium leather at mass-production scale may be within reach, according to new research from VTT Technical Research Center of Finland. The team made leather-like sheets using a continuous process rather than slow-growing trays. The study appeared in ACS Applied Bio Materials in July 2026. Mycelium is the underground network of fibers below mushroom caps. Researchers see it as a promising animal-free material for bags, shoes, and clothing. The hard part has been making enough of it. Most mycelium materials grow in trays. Fungi spread across the tray until the fibers knit into one solid sheet. That works for small batches but cannot support mycelium leather at mass-production scale. The VTT team took a different path. They grew a fungus called Trichoderma reesei using submerged fermentation. That means the fungus grows in a nutrient-rich liquid inside a bioreactor. A bioreactor is a tank with controlled growing conditions. The result is a wet mycelium pulp. The researchers washed the pulp and mixed it with sorbitol and cellulose. Sorbitol is a sugar-based softener that keeps the sheet from becoming brittle. Cellulose is a plant fiber that adds strength. The formulas used nanofibrillated cellulose, which is cellulose broken into extremely fine fibers. Sorbitol acts as a plasticizer, an additive that makes materials more flexible. Together, they shape how the finished sheet feels and performs. The team then spread the mix into thin sheets and dried them. The result is a nonwoven fabric, meaning the fibers are bonded together rather than woven or knitted. The researchers could handle, cut, and sew it much like a regular textile. Strength matters for any leather substitute. Tests showed tensile strength of 11 to 19 megapascals (MPa), depending on how the mycelium was pretreated. That number measures how much pulling force a material handles before it breaks. The sheets also stretched about 9% to 10% before fracturing. That flexibility matters for products like bags and shoes, which bend and flex every day. Scale was the real test. The team adapted a roller system similar to those used in paper manufacturing. It produced continuous sheets about 8 inches wide and 26 feet long. That is roughly the width of a letter-size page and the length of a large moving truck. The team used a roll-to-roll pilot line and a wet-casting process. Wet casting means spreading liquid pulp into a thin layer that dries into a sheet. It is still a pilot run. But it shows that mycelium leather at mass-production scale can move past small lab samples. Researchers in Finland used liquid fermentation and a roller line to bring mycelium leather at mass-production scale closer to reality. Photo by Cottonbro Studio on Pexels. Using familiar equipment could matter as much as the material itself. Manufacturers might not need to build entirely new production lines from scratch. That could lower the cost and risk of trying a new material. Co-author Manuel Arias-Barrantes said the work solves a major bottleneck in large-scale, affordable production. He noted that scalable options remain limited today. The pulp approach also gives researchers more control over the final material. They can adjust its properties, add color and texture, or layer it onto cotton fabric. The recipe is easy to change, opening the door to different products. The researchers sewed a prototype accessory bag from black-dyed mycelium fabric. It shows the material can take color and hold stitching. That is a practical first step toward real products. Why does this matter for shoppers? Many vegan leathers are made from petroleum-based plastics that are difficult to recycle. Animal leather also has environmental costs, including livestock and chemical processing. Géza Szilvay of VTT said the process uses renewable feedstocks and mild conditions. It involves no livestock and no chemically intensive steps. He believes the concept could become a viable alternative to non-renewable synthetic leathers, and scaling mycelium leather to mass production is central to that goal. Researchers describe the finished fabric as compostable. That could give it an advantage over plastic-based options at the end of a product’s life. It also supports a wider shift toward materials made from renewable sources. See also: Converting Kombucha to Green Textiles for Sustainable Fashion Questions remain. Mycelium materials still need further development to meet the demands of tough, everyday uses. Long-term durability and cost at factory volume will need testing. Mycelium is not the only plant-based option under study. Brands are also exploring leathers made from cactus and pineapple leaves. Several clothing companies already use pineapple leaf material in garments. Still, the study offers a clear path forward. A handbag grown in a tank and dried on a roller line no longer sounds far-fetched. If later tests hold up, mycelium leather at mass-production scale could give brands a renewable option made with familiar equipment. The post Mycelium Leather at Mass-Production Scale Moves Closer to Reality appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Festive decorations bring colour and warmth to a home, but a little greenery can make the space feel even more inviting. If you want to give your living room, entrance, or balcony a fresh look this festive season, tall indoor plants are a lovely way to do it. They add height, fill empty corners, and bring a natural charm to your decorations. Pair them with earthen pots, warm fairy lights, or a few diyas , and these plants can become part of your festive decor. Here are 10 tall houseplants worth considering. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lazy Gardener (@lazygardener.in) 1. Rubber Plant With its broad, glossy leaves and upright growth, the rubber plant makes a striking addition to any room. Its deep green foliage looks particularly beautiful against light-coloured walls. It prefers bright, indirect light and watering when the top layer of soil dries out. The rubber plant makes a striking addition to any room. Photograph: (Leaf Envy) 2. Bird of Paradise Known for its large, banana-like leaves, the bird of paradise brings a tropical feel indoors. Given enough light and space, it can grow quite tall. Place it near a bright window and water when the soil begins to dry. Known for its large, banana-like leaves, the bird of paradise brings a tropical feel indoors. Photograph: (Plant Drop) 3. Money Tree The money tree is loved for its distinctive braided trunk and clusters of green leaves. Usually associated with prosperity and good fortune, it makes a fitting addition to festive homes. It grows well in bright, indirect light and prefers well-draining soil. The money tree is loved for its distinctive braided trunk and clusters of green leaves. Photograph: (Patch Plants) 4. Areca Palm Its arching, feathery fronds give the areca palm a soft, tropical appearance. It works particularly well in living rooms and near entrances where it has room to spread. Keep it in bright, indirect light and maintain lightly moist soil. Its arching, feathery fronds give the areca palm a soft, tropical appearance. Photograph: (Amazon.in) 5. Monstera The monstera stands out for its large, naturally split leaves. Its dramatic foliage adds character without requiring complicated decoration. It prefers bright, indirect light and moderate watering . Give it a moss pole or support as it grows. The monstera stands out for its large, naturally split leaves. Photograph: (unlimitedgreens) 6. Fiddle Leaf Fig With its oversized, violin-shaped leaves, the fiddle leaf fig makes a beautiful statement plant. It looks especially elegant in a simple ceramic planter. Place it in a bright spot with indirect sunlight and avoid moving it around frequently. With its oversized, violin-shaped leaves, the fiddle-leaf fig makes a beautiful statement plant. Photograph: (Mason Home) 7. Dracaena Dracaena varieties are known for their upright growth and attractive foliage. Some have slender leaves with colourful edges, making them a good choice for narrow corners. They prefer indirect light and need watering only when the soil starts drying out. Dracaena varieties are known for their upright growth and attractive foliage. Photograph: (Thursd) 8. Yucca The yucca's woody stem and pointed leaves give it a distinctive, sculptural appearance. It is a good option for those who prefer plants that need less frequent watering. Keep it near a sunny window and allow the soil to dry between waterings. The yucca's woody stem and pointed leaves give it a distinctive, sculptural appearance. Photograph: (Fourwalls) 9. Elephant Ear As the name suggests, elephant ear plants have enormous, heart-shaped leaves that instantly catch the eye. Their lush foliage brings a tropical touch to indoor spaces. They prefer bright, indirect light, humidity, and consistently moist, well-draining soil. As the name suggests, elephant ear plants have enormous, heart-shaped leaves that instantly catch the eye. Photograph: (Bloomica) 10. Croton If your festive decor needs a burst of colour, the croton is a wonderful choice. Its leaves feature captivating shades of green, yellow, orange, and red. It needs plenty of bright light to maintain its vibrant colours and should be watered when the topsoil begins to dry. If your festive decor needs a burst of colour, the croton is a wonderful choice. Photograph: (Nista) Whether you prefer the deep green leaves of a rubber plant or the colourful foliage of a Croton, these houseplants can give your home a festive makeover that lasts well beyond the celebrations. Choose plants according to the light and space available, dress up their pots, and let the greenery do the rest.

items.descriptionOriginal: Copy: For over five decades, his artwork found a place in millions of Indian homes, becoming a familiar sight across generations. Artist S.M. Srinivasan, who passed away at 86, was known for his paintings of deities, especially his two iconic depictions of Lord Venkateswara, which became widely recognised through calendars, posters and framed prints. Born in Kovilpatti, Tamil Nadu, Srinivasan studied up to Class 10 before learning the art of painting under renowned artist Kondaiah Raju. In 1970, he got a rare opportunity to observe and paint the idol at the Tirumala temple. He created two versions, one with elaborate ornaments and another without them. Approved by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD), his paintings were reproduced as calendars, posters and framed prints. Soon, his artwork became a familiar sight on calendars across India, finding its way into homes, shops and everyday spaces. For generations, these familiar images became part of India’s visual and cultural landscape. While many may not have known the artist behind them, his work remained a part of their everyday lives. #Srinivasan #SMSrinivasan #TirupatiBalaji #IndianArt [S.M. Srinivasan artist, Lord Venkateswara painting artist, Tirupati Balaji calendar image]
