items.title: Φανταζόμαστε τις ποώδεις πόλεις του μέλλοντος
items.titleOriginal: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία έχει εκδοθεί από κοινού από το Reasons to be Cheerful και το Outrider Foundation . Το 2012, ο Philip Wallisfurth ήθελε να σώσει ένα δέντρο. Πολίτες στο Άαχεν της Γερμανίας διαμαρτυρήθηκαν για τα σχέδια για ένα εμπορικό κέντρο που απειλούσε ένα δέντρο 150 ετών. Ο Wallisfurth, τότε ένας επίδοξος καλλιτέχνης του δρόμου, αναρωτήθηκε αν μπορούσε να χρησιμοποιήσει βρύα - αντί για τα συνηθισμένα του…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story has been co-published by Reasons to be Cheerful and the Outrider Foundation . I n 2012, Philip Wallisfurth wanted to save a tree. Citizens in Aachen, Germany, were protesting plans for a shopping center that threatened a 150-year-old tree. Wallisfurth , then an aspiring street artist, wondered if he could use moss — instead of his usual spray can — to support the campaign. He harvested moss from a local park, used yogurt as an adhesive and stuck two-meter-high letters onto the construction fence, spelling out “greener living.” The reactions surprised him. “People loved it,” he recalls. “Many took pictures and some spontaneously hung flowers in small vases onto the fence.” He had stumbled upon a medium that was soft, tactile and alive — and a natural way of occupying public space. YouTube tutorials suggested mixing moss with buttermilk in a blender, but the results disappointed him. Through trial and error with different mosses and yogurts, he developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti.” Artist Philip Wallisfurth developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti with moss.” Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth Two years later, whiskey maker Jack Daniel’s hired him for a campaign. In Cologne, Wallisfurth covered an eight-by-eight-meter wall with moss lettering, spelling out a motto he lives by: never give up trying to do what you really want to be happy Now an artist with international projects and a studio in Berlin, Wallisfurth, 42, mostly paints large, colorful murals and designs anamorphic installations, room-filling works that seem to change shape depending on the viewer’s perspective. But moss continues to appeal to him for several reasons. He feels it’s uniquely suited to transform uninspiring urban spaces into places that feel more welcoming — and it has environmental benefits, too. He learned from speaking with scientists that moss can convert carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide into oxygen. “It also acts as a natural air filter and absorbs noise,” he notes. Moss continues to appeal to Wallisfurth for its ability to make spaces more welcoming and its environmental benefits. Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth There are more than 13,000 recognized species of moss. The unassuming plant that most homeowners would like to scrape off their driveways offers more than unusual shades of green. It can retain moisture, dampen sound and, under the right conditions, help regulate the temperature of the surfaces it covers. Wallisfurth dreams of turning entire structures — for instance, train stations — into buildings where moss improves the air and atmosphere. As cities grapple with increasingly dangerous heat, Wallisfurth’s artistic experiments intersect with a serious question for architects and climate researchers: While concrete, asphalt and masonry store the sun’s energy, cities are searching for ways to keep buildings and public spaces cooler. Could this small, overlooked plant become part of the answer? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Moss is remarkably adaptable. It has no conventional root system but absorbs moisture directly through its surface and can tolerate long periods of dehydration. A 2026 field study in Seoul showed moss-based green roofs reduced peak roof-surface temperatures by about 19° Celsius and maximum indoor temperatures by 2 to 3.5° Celsius during heat waves, while a 2026 peer-reviewed study from TU Delft in the Netherlands found that hydrated moss can produce evaporative cooling and insulate underlying surfaces. Credit: Lukas Gojda / Shutterstock Moss is remarkably adaptable. It has no conventional root system but absorbs moisture directly through its surface and can tolerate long periods of dehydration. It can retain moisture, dampen sound and, under the right conditions, help regulate the temperature of the surfaces it covers. As promising as these findings are, the reality is more complex than a green coating that simply cools whatever it covers. According to the Dutch researchers, the cooling effect only lasts as long as the moss is hydrated. Crucially, they found that dry moss exposed to direct sun can actually become warmer than bare mortar. So the question changes: Can cities engineer walls and roofs with moss that stays moist when cities most need cooling? Several startups are betting that the solution lies in redesigning the surfaces themselves. In London, Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels to turn city walls into living infrastructure. Founder and architect Nicky Naidu wants to change how the construction industry thinks about moss, which is often treated as a sign of neglect. “Moss gets a bad rep. But moss has intrinsic beauty, and we want to bring that beauty to cities,” Naidu told Reuters . “It’s carbon negative, bioreceptive, cost-effective and fire-safe. Everything that the industry needs and requires.” The company’s panels are made of a base material Naidu describes as bioreceptive concrete designed to support the growth of moss. The living wall systems incorporate controlled irrigation, delivering moisture directly rather than relying on rainfall or conventional surface spraying. Naidu argues that the moss walls are easier to maintain than conventional green walls because moss needs no soil to flourish. Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels to turn city walls into living infrastructure. Courtesy of Alive Labs In the Netherlands, Respyre has developed a similar concept with “Mosscrete,” a bioreceptive concrete that can be seeded with moss and also features an “ integrated, automated irrigation system that keeps the moss sufficiently hydrated, particularly during warmer and drier periods .” Both companies have moved from the prototype stage to making their panels commercially available. In Berlin, Green City Solutions built the world’s first vertical moss farm on 1,200 square meters to grow moss for sustainable air filters. The next step for the industry is to measure results in real life under varying temperatures and conditions, to determine where moss performs well enough to justify the investment. Not every experiment requires new materials or elaborate infrastructure. In Santiago de Compostela, Spain, a chance observation during the pandemic led city officials and university researchers to reconsider the vegetation growing between the city’s paving stones, including moss. After thermal cameras showed that stone surfaces with these small patches of greenery measured up to 25° Celsius cooler than bare paving, the city opted to leave the “urban microgreen” in place as a low-cost way to mitigate heat. A Respyre test panel after irrigation. Courtesy of Respyre Philip Wallisfurth keeps experimenting with the greenery, too. For a temporary installation, he transformed an entire living room in Berlin into an otherworldly moss-covered landscape. Again, he noticed people’s positive reaction. “The smell simply calmed people down,” he observed. “If you had a living moss wall in an office that was regularly watered, it would create an incredibly pleasant working climate. Plus, it filters the air and absorbs noise — it’s actually dreamlike.” Wallisfurth learned that most conventional moss art one finds in rooms is made from moss that has been dried and preserved with chemicals, eliminating the need to water it but also killing most of its environmental benefits. “It’s dead,” he says. His own bio-art has limits. Without preservation, the moss typically dries and dies within three to six months, depending on the surrounding dryness and acidity. “Like street art,” Wallisfurth notes, “it’s impermanent, too.” The walls of a bank building in Utrecht before and after renovation with Respyre’s bioreceptive concrete. Courtesy of Respyre But learning more about moss also made him reconsider where his material comes from. His sister, a nature guide, calls moss the “lungs of the forest” and told him it was wrong to take moss from forests and public spaces. He now sources his moss from an abandoned army training ground that is likely to soon be a construction site. His desire to create sustainable moss installations sometimes clashes with his clients’ expectations. Several big corporations approached him about creating moss pieces, he says, only to dismiss his concerns about sustainable sourcing. “They told me: ‘We don’t care. It just needs to look green in the pictures.’” He shakes his head. “That was a downer. It showed that most people only look at it as a means to an end.” The exchange captures a broader risk in the rush to make cities greener: The living material can become a visual shorthand for sustainability, even when its environmental value has not been proven. It might look green but actually be greenwashing. Credit: CinemaPhoto / Shutterstock “If you had a living moss wall in an office that was regularly watered, it would create an incredibly pleasant working climate. Plus, it filters the air and absorbs noise — it’s actually dreamlike.” –Philip Wallisfurth In addition to making his own moss art, Wallisfurth enjoys running moss workshops for kids at schools. Children love to experiment with the soft, tactile material, he says. Growing up in a rural part of the Eifel in Germany, he remembers walking barefoot across moss, and nature was his refuge when his own childhood was marked by loss. His parents died of cancer when he was young, and his brother was killed when Wallisfurth was only 14. He trained as a foreign-language correspondent and hotel manager before moving to Berlin and pursuing art. He turned to art explicitly as a means to brighten places up and turn rooms into positive spaces. “That’s what drives me,” he says. “Positivity is simply a much better way to deal with things. Of course, not everything is positive, but I have to try to stay positive.” His favorite projects begin with dark, inhospitable places and turn them into areas where people like to spend time. “That’s my goal as an artist.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime He believes he wouldn’t be an artist without his biography. And he sees a similar resilience in the plants: “A specialist once told me I could put moss in the oven at 270° Celsius, and if I water it afterward, it will come back to life.” In that way, he says, “Maybe I’m a little like moss. You can destroy it, but it simply grows again. It’s a fighter.” The post Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: 'Ελα μαζί μου. Σε πήρα».
items.titleOriginal: 'Come With Me. I Got You.'
items.description: Τριάντα χρόνια αφότου η μητέρα της πέθανε ξαφνικά ενώ υπηρετούσε στο Ειρηνευτικό Σώμα, η Κέιτ Ρόγκαν εξακολουθεί να κουβαλά τη μνήμη ενός ξένου που συνάντησε τη θλίψη της με τέσσερις ήσυχες λέξεις: «Έλα μαζί μου. Σε πήρα». Η γυναίκα καθοδήγησε τον Ρόγκαν από ένα προσγειωμένο αεροπλάνο, μέσω μιας πτήσης που ακυρώθηκε, σε μια νύχτα ξενοδοχείου και μέχρι την αγκαλιά της αδερφής της στο baggage cla…
items.descriptionOriginal: Thirty years after her mother died suddenly while she was serving in the Peace Corps, Kate Rogan still carries the memory of a stranger who met her grief with four quiet words: "Come with me. I got you." The woman guided Rogan off a grounded plane, through a canceled flight, through a hotel night, and all the way to her sister's arms at baggage claim - then disappeared, nameless, into ordinary life. What stays is not just the kindness, but what Rogan came to understand about herself in that moment: "I was this strong, independent young woman, but in that moment, I could not handle life without somebody helping me." Some losses crack us open in ways that expose how much we need each other, and some strangers seem to know this before we do.

Η πόλη του 1 τετραγωνικού μιλίου, που βρίσκεται ακριβώς απέναντι…
items.descriptionOriginal: Getting your daily steps in may be a little easier if you live in Hoboken, New Jersey. Earlier this month, Architectural Digest released a list of the nine most walkable cities in the U.S. based on recent studies, Redfin’s Walk Score tool, and consultations with realtors, residents, and tourism experts. The 1-square-mile city, which sits just across the Hudson River from downtown Manhattan, earned the top spot due to its ample public transportation and dense street grid. It received a 97 out of 100 on Walk Score, which measures the ability for residents to run errands and access amenities without a car — factors that can go a long way for physical health, mental health, and the health of the planet. View this post on Instagram “[Walkability] can benefit everything from household finances and health to the environment and overall quality of life,” Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, told the outlet. She added: “Walkable neighborhoods also create more opportunities for people to interact with local businesses, use public spaces and resources, and connect with their neighbors.” Science backs up those benefits. A 2021 paper showed higher walkability was associated with lower mortality rates in a cohort of 13,832 women. And a 2020 study of over 31,000 adults found that those living in high-walkability areas were 150% more likely to engage in adequate levels of physical activity and 76% less likely to be obese. Additionally, research from 2013 suggested that participants who walked more in their neighborhood experienced improved social interactions and felt more social cohesion within the community. RELATED: How 11,000 Twins Helped Illustrate the Importance of Making Cities Walkable In terms of the planet, Elizabeth Sawin, director of the Multisolving Institute, a research organization focused on climate change, equity, health, well-being, and biodiversity, summed up the power of walkability in a 2024 interview with Grist: “Every trip taken on foot instead of by a fossil fuel-powered car reduces greenhouse gas emissions.” Here’s the full list of America’s most walkable cities from Architectural Digest : 1. Hoboken, New Jersey 2. West Hollywood, California 3. Boston, Massachusetts 4. San Francisco, California 5. New York, New York 6. Washington, D.C. 7. Chicago, Illinois 8. Miami, Florida 9. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

Η ανθρωπότητα ανέβασε την ένταση σε ολόκληρο τον πλανήτη. Αυτό s…
items.descriptionOriginal: Every geological epoch leaves signatures. One of the Anthropocene’s may be a noise. Oceans echo with the drone of ship engines and blasts of sonar. Cities and suburbs roar with speeding cars and revving motorcycles. Even remote wilderness hums with passing airplanes and strolling hikers. Humanity has turned up the volume on the whole planet. That soundtrack is far reaching. New research in Science finds that noise pollution more than doubles death rates among wild animals. It is also rewriting the rules of who eats whom. In noisy places, prey grow jumpy and predators go hungry. Sometimes an animal fleeing the din runs straight into danger. Noise, the authors write, “reshapes the acoustic arms race” between species, and it creates winners and losers. The researchers argue that protecting wildlife in the Anthropocene means protecting quiet. “This work shows that noise pollution is an underrated threat to wildlife worldwide,” said Hansjoerg Kunc , an ecologist at Queen’s University Belfast and the paper’s lead author. Soundscapes, he said, should be safeguarded with the same seriousness as forests, wetlands and other physical habitats. Scientists have long known that noise harms living things. The World Health Organization calls it a serious health hazard for people: it shortens lives, impairs children’s brain development and disrupts sleep. In wildlife, noise has been shown to spike stress hormones in freshwater fish, alter feeding behavior , and cause forest dwellers to flee in panic . .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby What was missing was the big picture. Kunc and Queen’s colleague Rouven Schmidt gathered 214 studies examining noise effects on 177 species across six continents, from tiny beetles to hulking whales. They focused on controlled experiments, which can more reliably pin effects on noise itself. The effects were widespread. Noise was tied to fetal deformities, weakened immune systems and elevated stress hormones. It altered body size, feeding and parenting, and it changed animals’ success at hunting or escaping hunters. Pooled across the experiments, noise raised mortality by 138%. If 10 in every 100 animals would die in a world without human noise, 24 would die in a world with it. That’s large enough, the authors say, to “threaten population viability.” The effects on how species interact may matter just as much. Animals tended to steer clear of noisy areas, so their numbers there were 37% lower. The prey that remained were on high alert. So predators in noisy places caught 25% less prey, even though they worked harder to find it. But noise doesn’t necessarily help prey either. A loud sound might send a prey animal into a burrow or other enclosed space to hide. Those close quarters can amplify the noise, and that can flush the animal back into the open, where a predator is waiting. The fix, the researchers suggest, starts with treating sound as part of habitat. Kunc points to “measures such as low-noise zones that give animals a genuine acoustic refuge.” In an epoch defined by human influence, quiet may be one of the habitats most worth saving. items.title: Τι Διαβάζουμε: Μια πλαστική σακούλα 80 σεντ σώζει ζωές μητέρων
items.titleOriginal: What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives
items.description: Καλώς ήρθατε πίσω στην εβδομαδιαία μας ματιά στα παρασκήνια για το τι κάνει να μιλάει η ομάδα μας. Πείτε μας τι έχετε διαβάσει στο info@reasonstobecheerful.world και ίσως το παρουσιάσουμε εδώ. Στην τσάντα Μια παρέμβαση χαμηλού κόστους και χαμηλής τεχνολογίας σώζει ζωές σε μαιευτήρια σε όλη την Αφρική. Όπως αναφέρουν οι New York Times σε μια ιστορία που μοιράστηκε το Contributing…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. In the bag A low-cost, low-tech intervention is saving lives in maternity wards across Africa. As the New York Times reports in a story shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas, the maternal drape is a plastic pouch that can be used to easily measure blood loss. This allows health workers to act quickly in the case of postpartum hemorrhage, which is extremely dangerous. When combined with the necessary treatments, this intervention cut deaths by postpartum hemorrhage by about two-thirds. “The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite,” Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano, Nigeria, told the Times . “It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems.” Michaela says: I had no idea a simple, low-cost plastic bag is saving so many mothers’ lives. Bird’s-eye view In a lighter (but just as surprising) story of lives being saved, googly-eyed buoys are helping prevent seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. According to a Mongabay story that caught the attention of Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, these devices scare the birds away from the fishing gear. A study off Cornwall, England, found that nets fitted with kites shaped like birds of prey had 71 percent lower odds of catching seabirds, and nets with spinning “looming-eye” buoys had 59 percent lower odds. Becca says: I kinda love these “googly-eyed buoys,” despite their uncanny resemblance to Clippy the paperclip . What else we’re reading The fix for America’s terrible internet is hiding in Tennessee — shared by RTBC Founder David Byrne from Vox What If a Crisis Pregnancy Center Was Pro-Choice? — shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby from The Cut The planet’s vital signs are getting worse. One of the easiest fixes is your diet. — shared by Michaela Haas from Grist In other news… Just after last week’s historic midterm elections, we wrapped up The Depolarization Series , an exploration of the many ways people are defying division and really listening to those who disagree with them. You can check out the full series here — and don’t miss the many fantastic videos we shared on Instagram. The post What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: Επιπλέον καρέκλες στο Driveway

items.description: Στο Fargo της Βόρειας Ντακότα, ο Prakash Mathew και η σύζυγός του Jane είχαν έναν όμορφο κήπο που οι άνθρωποι συχνά σταματούσαν να θαυμάσουν. Σκέφτηκαν να γράψουν τα ονόματα των επισκεπτών τους και χαιρετούσαν τον καθένα ονομαστικά την επόμενη φορά. Με την πάροδο του χρόνου, παρείχαν επιπλέον καρέκλες και κάλεσαν τους ανθρώπους να καθίσουν και να συνομιλήσουν, και ένα διαφορετικό είδος κήπου εμφανίστηκε. «Όταν πήγαμε για το δικό μας…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Fargo, North Dakota, Prakash Mathew and his wife Jane had a beautiful garden people would often stop to admire. They made a point of writing down their visitors' names and would greet each by name the next time. Over time, they provided extra chairs and invited people to sit and chat, and a different kind of garden emerged. "When we went for our walks, we could hardly walk two blocks without stopping and talking to someone." Jane died suddenly in December of last year. When summer came, Prakash continued to go to the driveway, and people still joined him. He asked, "What if we did this — sat in my driveway, but intentionally, every other week, with a topic?" Everybody loved it. Driveway Dialogues was born. A neighborhood spirit had been planted, "with a garden, a few extra chairs in front of the house, and a curiosity to care for others."

items.descriptionOriginal: The year I turned 30, I moved to a peaceful neighborhood on Los Angeles’ Westside. I was 10 minutes from Venice Beach and had an apartment all to myself. The only catch (besides street parking)? It was 450 square feet. A couple of friends helped me optimize the place: We assembled a custom Murphy bed, installed a wall-mounted folding table, and chose decor that made it feel joyful and airy. Though I lamented not having more space at times, I discovered that my scaled-down quarters came with some perks. Styling the studio so intentionally felt empowering, and because it was so small, I often enjoyed my meals out in the courtyard under the sun. Years later, despite having married and moved into a comfortable condo, I still occasionally yearn for more square footage, particularly during dinner parties or when family visits for the holidays. To refresh my perspective, I spoke to interior design experts and therapists who helped illuminate some of the unexpected benefits of having a smaller home — and offered tips for making the most of yours. Benefits domin_domin—iStock/Getty Images Plus Cost and Cleaning We’ll start with perhaps the most obvious but still occasionally overlooked perks: “Less square footage means less time cleaning and organizing. Owning less means spending less time managing and maintaining your belongings,” Phoenix-based interior designer Mackenzie Collier explained in an email to Nice News. “That frees up more time for hobbies, socializing, and anything else you’d rather be doing!” She added that smaller spaces force us to be more thoughtful about what we buy and why (a welcome mindset shift for many), and that the money we save on quantity can be used to invest in quality — e.g., well-built furniture, bespoke decor, art. And it’s not just our shopping carts that feel the difference, Sierra Troitsky , an interior designer in Indianapolis, pointed out. “Smaller spaces are often more economical and environmentally friendly as they cost less to heat and cool,” she said. Mental Well-Being Less square footage can contribute to a greater sense of well-being because it can encourage us to be neat and organized, “which is calming for the brain,” said Sipora Weissman , a licensed therapist in Ventura, California. In a tiny room, a pile of unfolded laundry is a lot more noticeable than in a large one, for example, so we may be more inclined to actually, you know, put it away . “As a therapist who works with adults who get overstimulated easily, living in a small space can be overwhelming or it can actually be very supportive to someone’s nervous system,” Weissman explained. “If you fill that small space with tchotchkes and clutter, that will be a recipe for an unsettled brain. There are many scientific studies that show the negative impacts of clutter on the brain. But if you take this small space living situation as an opportunity, it can be very conducive to your mental health.” More Intentional Decor Just as I experienced when decorating my tiny quarters, less to work with can have a focusing effect. “A small living room lends itself to intentional decorating because you’re forced to narrow in on fewer, impactful pieces that set the tone for the space — say, a beautiful sofa, a well-sized rug, task and accent lighting, and some meaningful artwork,” said Elena Navarro, an interior designer and professional organizer at Sparkly Maid Austin . View this post on Instagram She added: “I love that limited square footage forces you to really think through everything that you bring in the door, from new dishes to cozy throw blankets to holiday decor. Where is the item going to live? Do you use it enough to warrant giving it a permanent home?” Better for Gathering and Bonding The reason celebrity chef Ina Garten considers six people the ideal number for a dinner party is the same reason your modest home might lend itself to more meaningful gatherings: intimacy. “Small group events tend to produce an environment that allows for more personalized conversation,” explained Whitney Willborn , a Texas-based licensed clinical social worker, adding that it’s easier to not only include everyone in the conversation but also to spot when others appear to be excluded. If guests are spread out in different rooms or fragmented into groups, it’s trickier to notice when a new friend is standing awkwardly by themself, for example. Your own family might benefit from a smaller floor plan, too. Collier recently moved out of a 900-square-foot home, and her household has experienced some nostalgia for the cozier living situation. “There was nowhere to escape to, so we’d sit together, watch a movie, or play games,” she said. “Those shared moments became some of our favorite memories.” Spend More Time in Community My al fresco dining habit of yore highlights how the wide world can beckon when your indoors isn’t vast. Collier had the same experience. “I’ve found that living in a small space encourages me to spend more time outdoors and in my community,” she shared. “Whether it was tending to my garden, or heading to a local coffee shop to work, living small naturally pushed me to get out into the community more.” Tips Double Duty Interior designer Preeti Shah made her name in New York, where minuscule apartments are no big deal (one of the tiniest is an infinitesimal 55 square feet !). When she moved to an area of Houston filled with massive homes, she was bemused. At around 3,000 square feet, her house is among the smallest — yet she said it’s where her neighborhood pals prefer to hang out. Courtesy of Preeti Shah Shah’s lounge area with convertible coffee-to-dining room table A design principle Shah prioritizes, in any sized space, is double duty. “Anything I purchase, I would like for my client to be able to use it in more than just one way,” she shared. Ottomans are great for seating and storage, twin beds can become kings when guests stay over, and dining chairs should be comfy enough to be used as additional living room seating. In her own house, rather than a dining room table that sits unused, she opted for a convertible coffee table that lifts and extends to seat 10. Size and Amount Matter Troitsky explained that getting furniture that’s sized correctly can help a lot with how large your home feels (e.g., an enormous couch in a tiny bedroom might make the space seem small). But that doesn’t mean you should automatically purchase miniature versions of everything you’d buy for a bigger area. “It’s best to take inventory of what you actually use, need, and love, and start there,” Navarro said. She added: “For holiday decor, instead of trying to deck out every inch of your small living space, pick one or two areas to really lean into — the Christmas tree, the mantel, the coffee table, etc.” Get Comfortable With Borrowing Why use up valuable storage space on extra glassware and guest seating for your one annual holiday get-together when you can call a friend and ask to borrow theirs? As a bonus, it gives you both an excuse for a visit. Another option is to rent what you need when you need it. Ultimately, do your best to remember that, as Navarro put it, “the goal is always to make your guests feel at home — not to impress them with how big your place is!” RELATED: Make Your Home Happier With These Dopamine-Inducing Decorating Tips

items.title: Μεγέθυνση: 12 Standouts από τη σύντομη λίστα Φωτογράφου της Χρονιάς από κοντά
items.titleOriginal: Zoom In: 12 Standouts From the Close-Up Photographer of the Year Shortlist
items.description: Η καλύτερη φωτογραφία σας κάνει να επιβραδύνετε και να παρατηρήσετε κάτι που διαφορετικά θα μπορούσε να αγνοηθεί — και οι φιναλίστ για την όγδοη έκδοση του Close-Up Photographer of the Year κάνουν ακριβώς αυτό. Οι εικόνες που προκρίθηκαν μόλις αποκαλύφθηκαν από ένα ρεκόρ 15.388 υποβολών σε 11 κατηγορίες. Το παραπάνω πλάνο, με τίτλο «Χρυσή σκόνη», είναι ένα από τα επίμαχα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The best photography makes you slow down and notice something that might otherwise go overlooked — and the finalists for the eighth edition of Close-Up Photographer of the Year do just that. The shortlisted images were just revealed out of a record 15,388 submissions across 11 categories. The above shot, titled “Golden dust,” is one of the contenders in the animals category and features a Eurasian hoopoe taking a dust bath outside of Aurangabad, India. The dust helps remove excess oil from the bird’s feathers so they don’t stick together, but according to photographer Sarthak Agrawal, the swirling particles also make a good shot “especially difficult” (and thus especially impressive). “This year’s shortlist is a fabulous showcase of imagination, technical expertise, and natural curiosity,” competition co-founder Tracy Calder said in a press release shared with Nice News. The top 100 pics and the winning photographers will be announced in January, but submissions aren’t closed just yet. The competition holds an adjacent challenge that follows a specific theme, and this year’s is “Close to Home.” Hopeful shutterbugs of any age and skill level have until Nov. 30 to enter and Dec. 7 to upload their pics to the website. “Proving you don’t have to travel far to find something extraordinary,” the website states about the theme choice, which was voted on by the public. “We’re looking for close-up, macro, and micro photographs taken in a home and its immediate surroundings: the home’s rooms, outbuildings (such as sheds, garages, and greenhouses), garden, balcony, doorstep, or the street directly outside. This may be your own home or the home of family or friends.” Scroll to view a selection of the shortlisted images. Studio Art: “Rose Thorns” by Donald Bolak © Donald Bolak/CUPOTY “Fairly high level of magnification for a macro shot of a single rose thorn. The larger thorn is about 3/8 inch high. This is one of the things I enjoy most about macro — discovering sights unseen and unimagined. In this case a slightly surreal and alien landscape where rose thorns can be mountain peaks.” Young: “A Little Punky” by Oliver Lacey © Oliver Lacey/CUPOTY “I photographed this male Green Jumping Spider (Mopsus mormon) with its characteristic (and rather impressive) mohawk hairstyle in my suburban backyard in Brisbane, Australia.” Invertebrate Portrait: “Isopod portrait” by Adam Ferry © Adam Ferry/CUPOTY “I found this woodlouse resting underneath a piece of bark in a local woodland in Surrey, England. As it was fairly cold the woodlouse remained perfectly still allowing me to capture this focus stack of 80 photos. I love the high level of detail I could due to the increased magnification as the portrait filled most of the frame.” Underwater: “Rockpool Sanctuary” by Lisa Skelton © Lisa Skelton/CUPOTY “Young elephant seal pups or ‘weaners’ gather around natural rock pools on the Falkland Islands, using the protected waters to practice swimming and diving until they are ready to venture out to sea.” Intimate Landscape: “Where Worlds Collide” by Johannes Kowalewski © Johannes Kowalewski/CUPOTY “High above the Baltic Sea, an ancient beech forest glows in autumn colorrs atop the dramatic white chalk cliffs of Jasmund National Park on the island of Rügen, Germany.” Animals: “Nosepick” by Steffen Foerster © Steffen Foerster/CUPOTY “A blackish cinclodes or tussock-bird (Cinclodes antarcticus) picks at the nose of a resting southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) on Sea Lion Island, in the Falkland Islands.” Insects: “Spoonwing” by Lucien Harris © Lucien Harris/CUPOTY “I followed this spoonwing for over 10 minutes as it clumsily flew along the border of an overgrown field in the Peloponnese region of Greece, waiting for the perfect backdrop to compose a photo of this beautiful creature.” Underwater: “Fish Out of Context” by Marco Domenicucci © Marco Domenicucci/CUPOTY “A shoal of goldfish swim in an urban pond inside a metropolitan business district. Two worlds divided by a thin waterline: glass and concrete above and an aquatic ecosystem below.” Young: “Fight for the Perfect Fishing Spot” by Sasha Jumanca © Sasha Jumanca/CUPOTY “I managed to photograph these two blue kingfishers in December while they were defending their fishing territory in Schlosspark Nymphenburger, Munich. They faced each other directly and even tried to push one another under the water, showing how they compete for the best spots. This kind of behavior is quite rare, as kingfishers usually defend their territory by calling or chasing each other, rather than through physical contact.” Intimate Landscape: “Untitled 14” by Lukas Furlan © Lukas Furlan/CUPOTY “I was already fascinated by this scene, but rotating the image later revealed an entirely different world, almost like looking through a portal. It’s a reminder of the magic of experimentation and unexpected discoveries in photography.” Animals: “Suspended” by Joao Pontes © Joao Pontes/CUPOTY “In Portugal, there is no reptile quite as remarkable as the chameleon. Every year, towards the end of summer, the Algarve fills with juvenile chameleons. Naturally discreet, they become more active as the sun climbs higher in the sky, setting off to explore the world around them. Here, at the edge of the ocean, they inhabit the coastal dunes. At their scale, the slender stems of sea pinks become towering lianas, suspended pathways through this sandy jungle. To capture this image, I used a fisheye lens, aiming for a composition that would reveal not only the chameleon itself, but also the perhaps unexpected habitat it calls home.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Going digital is often assumed to be a modern, efficient strategy that will save energy and resources: picture smart cities and industries humming along, with everything needed to run them stored cleanly in the cloud. The reality is just the opposite, according to a new study. Across 20 of the world’s largest economies, the growth of information technology has increased environmental burdens—largely because of the energy required to build and run digital infrastructure . In the new study, researchers gathered World Bank data on the G20 economies from 1990 through 2023. This group of large economies accounts for 80% of global GDP and 70% of carbon emissions. The researchers looked at three indicators of digitalization: internet usage, landline telephone subscriptions, and cellular subscriptions. They used a variety of statistical techniques to probe the direct and indirect associations between these indicators and carbon emissions. Past studies have established that information and communications technologies have yielded huge social and economic benefits for nations around the world, but the environmental consequences of these technologies have been less clear. All three indicators of digitalization are associated with higher carbon emissions, the researchers found. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , .IRPP_ruby:visited , .IRPP_ruby:active {border:0!important;}.IRPP_ruby .clearfix:after {content: "";display: table;clear: both;}.IRPP_ruby {display: block;transition: background-color 250ms;webkit-transition: background-color 250ms;width: 100%;opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: #eaeaea;}.IRPP_ruby:active , .IRPP_ruby:hover {opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: inherit;}.IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl {background-position: center;background-size: cover;float: left;margin: 0;padding: 0;width: 31.59%;position: absolute;top: 0;bottom: 0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {float: right;width: 65.65%;padding:0;margin:0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text {display: table;height: 130px;left: 0;top: 0;padding:0;margin:0;padding-top: 20px;padding-bottom: 20px;}.IRPP_ruby .IRPP_ruby-content {display: table-cell;margin: 0;padding: 0 74px 0 0px;position: relative;vertical-align: middle;width: 100%;}.IRPP_ruby .ctaText {border-bottom: 0 solid #fff;color: #0099cc;font-size: 14px;font-weight: bold;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .postTitle {color: #000000;font-size: 16px;font-weight: 600;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .ctaButton {background: url(https://www.anthropocenemagazine.org/wp-content/plugins/intelly-related-posts-pro/assets/images/next-arrow.png)no-repeat;background-color: #afb4b6;background-position: center;display: inline-block;height: 100%;width: 54px;margin-left: 10px;position: absolute;bottom:0;right: 0;top: 0;}.IRPP_ruby:after {content: "";display: block;clear: both;} Recommended Reading: The average Internet user spends 3,230 hours online every year. Here's the carbon footprint of that. Strikingly, this pattern was almost entirely due to direct effects—that is, the energy needed to build and power digital infrastructure. “Data centers, device connectivity, and communication networks consume significant amounts of energy, which is largely sourced from carbon-intensive electricity,” the researchers write. The results suggest that the environmental benefits of digitalization depend on green electricity to power it—and at a global scale, that shift largely hasn’t happened yet. Clean energy is well known to be a key factor in determining the environmental benefits of electric cars . That relationship might not be as obvious in the case of digital technologies—it’s easy to overlook the energy required to make bits and bytes go bopping around the planet—but it’s no less crucial, the new work shows. The researchers expected that the early stages of digitalization, such as land line phone use, would be associated with increasing environmental burden but later stages, represented by internet and cellular adoption, with reduced carbon emissions—a pattern known as an environmental Kuznets curve. “In fact, economic and digital expansion continue to increase emissions rather than reduce them in the G20, revealing that these economies prioritize higher production and income over the cleaner environmental trajectory they often claim to pursue,” the researchers write. The upshot is that a push for digitalization needs to be accompanied by an effort to decarbonize the electricity that powers digital technologies, the researchers argue. Going forward, they say, governments should evaluate digitalization efforts not just in terms of technology access but also in terms of their climate impacts. Source: Alabdulwahab S. et al. “ ICT and CO2 Emissions in the G20: A Channel-Based Mediation Analysis .” Sustainability 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

items.title: Τι θα γινόταν αν σταματήσαμε να αντιμετωπίζουμε την κοινωνική περίθαλψη σαν υπηρεσία;
items.titleOriginal: What if we Stopped Treating Social Care like a Service?
items.description: Στο Botton Village στο βόρειο Γιορκσάιρ, ένας ερευνητής φιλοσοφίας επισκέπτεται έναν παλιό του φίλο και βρίσκει κάτι που δεν περίμενε: έναν άντρα που μεταμορφώθηκε. Ο Μαξ, ο οποίος δυσκολευόταν να βρει τη βάση του σε συμβατικές ρυθμίσεις περίθαλψης, μετακινείται στην κοινότητα Camphill Esk Valley με αυτό που ο φίλος του περιγράφει ως «μια σταθερή ευκολία που δεν είχα δει πριν…
items.descriptionOriginal: At Botton Village in North Yorkshire's moors, a philosophy researcher visits an old friend and finds something he didn't expect: a man transformed. Max, who had struggled to find his footing in conventional care arrangements, moves through the Esk Valley Camphill Community with what his friend describes as "a settled ease I hadn't seen in him before." His explanation is simple and quietly devastating: "It's been the best two years of my life. Much better than anything before." What the researcher gradually comes to understand - through months of shared meals, garden work, and community forums - is that Max hadn't just found better support. He had found a place where his presence mattered, where contribution and belonging were woven into the daily fabric of life rather than delivered on a schedule. The article raises a question that conventional social care policy rarely pauses long enough to ask: if what people most need is genuine community, what does it mean that we have built a system structurally designed to provide everything but that?

items.title: Τα κολέγια γίνονται δημιουργικά για να βοηθήσουν τους μαθητές με τα παιδιά
items.titleOriginal: Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία δημοσιεύτηκε αρχικά από το Open Campus. Περνώντας από το συμβουλευτικό γραφείο του New River μια μέρα, η Stephanie Addikis παρατήρησε ότι τα βιβλία ζωγραφικής και τα Lego που είχε βοηθήσει να αποθηκεύσουν σε ένα κοντινό κουτί ήταν… «πολύ αγαπημένα». Αυτό ακριβώς ήλπιζε ότι θα συμβεί. Το «απασχολημένο κουτί» με παιχνίδια είναι μέρος μιας νέας προσπάθειας στο New River για προμήθεια…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Open Campus . W alking by New River’s advising office one day, Stephanie Addikis noticed that the coloring books and Legos that she had helped stock in a nearby box were … “well-loved.” This was just what she was hoping would happen. The “busy box” stuffed with toys is part of a new effort at New River to support parenting students. When students are filling out the FAFSA or visiting with their adviser, they can bring their children and know they will have toys nearby to entertain them. “I don’t think we realized how many kids were coming on campus until we put these out, and now they’re really being utilized,” said Addikis, who is the adult career coach and community outreach specialist at New River. New River Community College is working to integrate more support for parenting students throughout campus. Courtesy of New River Community College A report released a couple weeks ago from The Institute for College Access & Success, or TICAS, showed that about a quarter of students attending rural-serving institutions are parents. But those colleges are also less likely to have childcare on campus than their non-rural counterparts. A lack of data on the number of parenting students is one of the biggest challenges for colleges trying to support them, according to one of the authors of that report, Erika Roberson. There’s a reason that Addikis was so excited to see used toys on campus: She does not know exactly how many parent students go to New River. While at least five states have now required public colleges to ask students if they have children, and Virginia just passed similar legislation this spring , the lack of standardized data collection makes serving these students even more difficult. And supporting them matters because student parents are more likely to be students of color, low-income and the first in their families to go to college. Those challenges combined make them less likely to graduate than their non-parenting peers. But, like rural places do, these colleges are getting creative in expanding support even with limited data and funding. To collect more thorough data, Roane State Community College in eastern Tennessee is partnering with Achieving the Dream . Others are collaborating with local churches, women shelters, groups like United Way and other nonprofits to connect student parents with resources. Our reporter at partner newsroom The Fort Worth Report, Dang Le, recently reported on new childcare centers that opened at Tarrant County College with the support of the college, county and a childcare nonprofit. “Not all these schools are receiving robust grants to do this work,” Roberson said. “Maybe there are existing partnerships that schools have that they might be able to tap into to more explicitly support their student parents, or maybe there are ways in which they can modify syllabi to include family-friendly policies that don’t have dollar signs on it.” Weighed down by negative news? Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Rather than one new program, it’s a cultural shift that student parents are looking for, according to another recent report focused on six public rural-serving colleges and universities in California . In other words, student parents want to feel seen — by their counselors, advisers, professors and other staff members or peers. While parents make up a large portion of students at rural-serving schools, it’s common for these students to still feel isolated . That’s why several colleges featured in the TICAS report are starting peer parenting groups and hosting events. New River, for example, has a dedicated family study room with child-sized furniture in their library (which also serves as a public library) and consistently hosts events or dinners for students and faculty with children. New River provides care packages for new and expecting parents, including diapers, wipes, a Walmart gift card and t-shirts. Courtesy of New River Community College Addikis said she felt this cultural shift even more prominently at New River when funding to parent-support programs decreased. New River was one of the first five colleges to receive the College Attainment for Parent Students grants from the Virginia Foundation for Community College Education. In those first couple of years, the college created cohorts of 20 student parents, and each parent was eligible for $2,000 stipends per semester, including summer semesters. Now, the foundation associated with the community college system gives each of the 23 schools some funding, so the grant amounts have decreased. New River adjusted by starting an application process, and they granted 17 students $500 each this year. Addikis said more than half of the students who applied said they rely on friends and family for childcare, so this stipend will likely help reimburse things like gas or food. But with fewer financial resources, Addikis started to look at what she could do to grow relationships with these student parents and remind them that they are not on their own. For example, she has a work-study student who is also a parent this semester, and that student is planning to start a student parent club on campus. The challenge, she said, still remains in increasing awareness about the resources on campus. One thing that she said helped was creating a section of their first-year orientation course specifically for adult learners and highlighting resources available for parents. “I see it now as a warm hug, and a lot of love and support and just a building of awareness,” she said, talking about how the parent support has changed with less funding. Join Cancel anytime Still, researchers like those at TICAS still advocate for increased data and funding for student parent support, especially on rural campuses. Two federal grant programs in particular focus on this area: Childcare Access Means Parents in Schools and Basic Needs for Postsecondary Students. “I don’t want policymakers to forget rural parenting students,” Roberson said. “And if policymakers are really interested in strengthening rural economies, I think it’s important that they also invest in rural parenting students.” The post Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: Νέα μελέτη δείχνει ότι οι «queer φιλίες» κάνουν καλό στην υγεία σας

items.description: Ερευνητές στο Πολιτειακό Πανεπιστήμιο του Μίσιγκαν και στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Κεντάκι βρήκαν συνδέσμους μεταξύ των συνομηλίκων LGTBQ+ και της ψυχικής τους ευεξίας.
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at Michigan State University and the University of Kentucky found links between LGTBQ+ peers and their mental well-being.

items.title: Δύο ψαράδες διασώζουν πιανίστα κρουαζιερόπλοιου που πέρασε εννέα ώρες περπατώντας νερό στη θάλασσα
items.titleOriginal: Two Fishermen Rescue Cruise Ship Pianist Who Spent Nine Hours Treading Water at Sea
items.description: Δύο ψαράδες μετέτρεψαν ένα συνηθισμένο πρωινό στο νερό σε μια σωτήρια διάσωση, αφού ανακάλυψαν ένα μέλος του πληρώματος κρουαζιερόπλοιου να πατάει νερό στον Ειρηνικό Ωκεανό, σχεδόν 20 μίλια μακριά από τις ακτές της Καλιφόρνια.
items.descriptionOriginal: Two fishermen turned an ordinary morning on the water into a life-saving rescue after discovering a cruise ship crew member treading water in the Pacific Ocean nearly 20 miles off the California coast.

items.title: Ο γάμος της ακυρώθηκε, έτσι προσκάλεσε 11 ξένους στην Ιρλανδία
items.titleOriginal: Her Wedding Was Canceled, So She Invited 11 Strangers to Ireland
items.description: Όταν ο αρραβώνας της Bridget Devaney τελείωσε μετά την επείγουσα ιατρική περίθαλψη του αρραβωνιαστικού της, έμεινε να κρατά σχέδια για ένα ταξίδι στη Βόρεια Ιρλανδία και μια ημέρα γάμου που δεν θα ερχόταν ποτέ. Αντί να τα εγκαταλείψει όλα, δημοσίευσε μια ανώνυμη πρόσκληση στα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης και 11 γυναίκες από τις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες, τον Καναδά και την Ουαλία είπαν ναι - σε έναν ξένο, μια χώρα, μια…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Bridget Devaney's engagement ended after her fianc 's medical emergency, she was left holding plans for a trip to Northern Ireland and a wedding day that would never come. Rather than abandon it all, she posted an anonymous invitation on social media, and 11 women from the United States, Canada, and Wales said yes - to a stranger, a country, and an uncertain week. "When these women signed up for this trip, they didn't know my name. They didn't know what I looked like. They didn't know anything about me," Bridget told BBC News NI. On the day originally reserved for her wedding, the women dressed up and stood together against Northern Ireland's coastline for photographs that captured something the original plans never could have. What the trip quietly reveals is how much people are willing to show up for one another -- and how belonging can find us even in the ruins of what we thought our lives would look like.
